after.title: Preprint: A five-day Mindfulness Based Intervention to reduce burnout and psychological distress in UK Medical Students
after.authors: Cromie, A.; Kaur, M.; Powell, N.; Brown, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Swansea University College of Medicine: Swansea University Medical School
after.abstract: Background Medical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout. Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs. UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments, however more research is required to investigate the efficacy of mindfulness for healthcare professionals and students.   Method Four cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention. Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online using validated outcome measures for burnout, psychological distress and wellbeing. Results Statistical analysis of data from 69 participants found a statistically significant improvement post intervention (T2) for current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001). Statistically significant improvements in psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up (T3). Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%. Discussion Medical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.

after.title: Preprint: Divergent Causes of Death After Ischemic and Hemorrhagic Stroke in the Reperfusion Era: A Contemporary Cohort Study
after.authors: Kadiyala, V.; Simpkins, A. N.; Chugh, H.; Czarny, R.; Uy-Evanado, A.; Bosson, N.; Tatonetti, N.; Reinier, K.; Chugh, S. S.
after.abstract: Background: Contemporary data on long-term, cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors are sparse, and much of the existing evidence derives from studies performed before the modern reperfusion era. We sought to characterize long-term cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors to discharge (differentiated by stroke subtype) when compared to in-hospital stroke decedents treated under contemporary standards of care. Methods: Using a hybrid billing-code/imaging and large language model-assisted chart-review pipeline, we identified adults hospitalized for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in the Observational Study of Cardiac Arrest Risk (OSCAR) cohort (Cedars-Sinai Health System, Los Angeles) between 2017 and 2020, followed through June 30, 2025. Cause of death was determined and classified into 10 categories. Results: Among 1,344 stroke patients (mean age 74.0 {+/-} 14.9 years; ischemic n=1,036 [77.1%], hemorrhagic n=308 [22.9%]), 203 (15.1%) did not survive the index stroke. Of the 1,141 discharged survivors, 625 (54.8%) died over a median follow-up of 5.2 years. Cerebrovascular causes predominated during index stroke hospitalization (36.0%) but accounted for only 15.5% of post-stroke discharge deaths. Among ischemic stroke survivors, cardiac disease was the leading cause of death (31.6%), with sudden cardiac arrest alone accounting for 10.9% of deaths. Among hemorrhagic stroke survivors, cancer (38.9%) was the leading cause of death. Despite these divergent cause-of-death profiles, overall survival did not differ significantly by subtype (median 5.5 vs 5.8 years; P=0.90). Conclusions: In this contemporary, reperfusion-era cohort, causes of death shifted from cerebrovascular predominance in the acute phase to heart disease/cardiac arrest after ischemic stroke, and malignancy after hemorrhagic stroke. These findings argue for development of subtype-specific post-stroke surveillance, including structured longitudinal cardiac and sudden-death risk assessment for ischemic stroke survivors.

after.authors: Pedersen, T. J.; Yu, J.; Li, A.; Ibanez, L.; Bubu, O. M.; Lucey, B. P.
after.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-{beta} plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau. Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist, was previously shown to acutely reduce the ratio of phosphorylated tau-181 to unphosphorylated tau-181 (pT181/T181) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, its effects on plasma pT181/T181 and broader proteomic networks remain unknown. Here, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg. Paired CSF and plasma samples were collected longitudinally via indwelling intrathecal and intravenous catheters. Plasma AD biomarkers were quantified by mass spectrometry, and proteomic profiling was performed using the SomaScan 11K assay on samples from hours 0, 16, and 24. Suvorexant increased pT181/T181 in plasma while decreasing it in CSF between 08:00 to 16:00. At the pathway level, suvorexant increased the extracellular abundance of proteins associated with translation, RNA binding, cytoskeletal organization and endosomal sorting, centrally at 16 hours and peripherally at 24 hours, and decreased cytokine and receptor-ligand signaling and serine protease activity in plasma at 24 hours. As plasma biomarkers are increasingly used for clinical screening and trial enrollment, factors that influence their levels, including medications, must be identified and their effects on interpretation understood.

after.authors: Enbar-Salo, N.; Palmer, P.; Munro, C.; Dubbelman, M. A.; Aaronson, A.; Nosheny, R.; Gatchel, J.; Marshall, G.; Vannini, P.; Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School. Department of Computer Science and Mathematics, Bowdoin College.
after.abstract: Background: Altered memory self-awareness is common in mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but its relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and progression remains unclear. Methods: Using 590 amnestic MCI ADNI participants, memory self-awareness was derived from participant-informant discrepancies on the memory subdomain of the Everyday Cognition questionnaire. Heightened awareness and unawareness subscores were calculated, and k-means clustering identified four phenotypes. Associations with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography (PET) were examined, and clinical progression was assessed using Cox models. Results: Aware and Unaware groups showed lower CSF amyloid-B, and higher CSF phosphorylated tau and PET amyloid. The Unaware phenotype was associated with increased progression risk (hazard ratio 2.41, 95% CI 1.48-3.92), whereas the Worried Well phenotype showed reduced risk (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.99). Conclusions: Multidimensional assessment of memory self-awareness identifies biologically and prognostically distinct subgroups within MCI and may improve risk stratification in prodromal AD.

after.title: Preprint: Germline Shelterin Loss of Function Predisposes to Lipoma and Uterine Leiomyoma: Population Evidence Bearing on Shelterin-Associated Sarcoma Risk
after.authors: Lin, B. D.; Chan, K. H.-L.; Zhang, Z.; Zhi, L.; Leow, A. Y.; Chi, J. C.; Zhou, M. Y.; Bui, N.; Ganjoo, K.; Pan, M.
after.abstract: Purpose Germline shelterin variants were linked to sarcoma in a case-enriched cohort. Whether shelterin loss of function predisposes to mesenchymal neoplasia in the general population is unknown. Methods We analyzed rare-variant collapsing associations for five shelterin genes across neoplasm phenotypes in UK Biobank exomes, with Genebass as a second pipeline. Prespecified shelterin and centrosome gene sets were tested by permutation-calibrated statistics against a TP53/RB1/NF1 positive control. Carrier risks were compared with telomere-lengthening predictions. Results Lipoma risk was increased in TERF1 (odds ratio [OR], 3.32; P = 8.4 x10-), POT1, and TERF2IP carriers, and uterine leiomyoma risk in all four core shelterin genes, most strongly POT1 (OR, 2.23; P = 4.0 x 10-); POT1 and TINF2 reproduced in Genebass. TERF1 was also associated with thyroid cancer and monoclonal gammopathy. Neither gene set nor the positive control was associated with self-reported sarcoma. Telomere lengthening accounted for POT1-associated chronic lymphocytic leukemia risk but not myeloma or TINF2-associated thyroid cancer, where observed risk exceeded prediction five- to seven-fold. Conclusion Shelterin loss of function is a population-level risk factor for lipoma and uterine leiomyoma, the benign counterparts of liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma. TERF1 joins POT1 and TINF2 as long-telomere cancer genes. Sarcoma-specific penetrance remains untested.

after.abstract: Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) catalyzes the hydration of C4-C6 acyl-CoA molecules to produce ATP in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Deficiency of the ECHS1 enzyme, ECHS1D, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that presents with a large and pleomorphic clinical spectrum. We present the largest comprehensive study of known diagnosed ECHS1D patients to date, reporting 26 new patients and 8 novel variants in conjunction with a literature review of 87 previously reported patients. All patients were categorized into neonatal, infantile, and late-onset groups based on age of onset and clinical course. Neonatal-onset cases were characterized by early and severe multisystem disease, often with lactic acidosis, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and high early mortality (62.5%). The infantile-onset group was heterogeneous, but many exhibited hallmark features such as dystonia, developmental delay, and basal ganglia involvement on neuroimaging. Mortality was significantly lower than the neonatal cohort (24.4%). Late-onset patients had more localized neurologic symptoms, particularly dystonia, and significantly lower mortality overall (0%). Moreover, we report a 37.5% survival rate in newly reported neonatal onset patients compared with 18.2% in prior reports, possibly reflective of earlier recognition of ECHS1D and greater utilization of therapies including N-acetylcysteine, sodium dichloroacetate, and valine-restricted diet.

after.title: Preprint: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
after.authors: Merchi, L.; Boucheham, C.; Layeb, A.; Derouiche, A.
after.abstract: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

after.title: Preprint: Formal dissent in CHMP opinions on new medicines, 2020-2025
after.authors: Siebert, M.; Tibau, A.
after.abstract: Disagreement within medicines regulation is rarely visible in the public record at the point an opinion is adopted. We examined divergent positions formally appended to opinions of the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) on new medicines from 2020 through 2025, both those opposing a positive opinion and those favoring authorization despite a negative opinion, describing how often they occurred, how large the dissenting minorities were, and which issues they raised. Divergent positions opposed 28 of 331 positive opinions (8.5%) and most often concerned efficacy and methodological limitations. Of 22 final negative opinions publicly available, 6 (27%) were accompanied by a divergent position favoring authorization. These records show when CHMP members disagreed about whether the evidence justified authorization. Indexing these disagreements and publishing vote outcomes with each opinion would make regulatory uncertainty visible and help clinicians, payers and health technology assessment bodies make better-informed decisions about treatment use and coverage.

after.title: Preprint: Routine Xpert MTB/XDR for Tuberculosis Drug-Resistance Surveillance in Northern Morocco: A Four-Year Programmatic Analysis
after.authors: Ez-Zari, A.; Boulaich, A.; Bouti, K.; Mennane, Z.; Elmtili, N.; Mezzoug, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Universite Abdelmalek Essaadi Faculte des Sciences
after.abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance requires diagnostic systems that can rapidly identify resistance beyond rifampicin and generate potentially actionable resistance information for routine public-health monitoring. We evaluated programmatic Xpert MTB/XDR use and characterized the molecular resistance profiles generated within a regional tuberculosis diagnostic network in northern Morocco. We retrospectively analyzed 258 Xpert MTB/XDR testing episodes performed from April 2022 to July 2026 and linked available Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra results with target-level molecular outputs. Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was detected in 203 episodes (78.7%), of which 188 (92.6%) had an interpretable rifampicin result. Molecular rifampicin resistance was detected in 75/188 episodes (39.9%) and isoniazid resistance in 71/192 (37.0%); molecular multidrug-resistant tuberculosis was identified in 51/184 (27.7%) episodes with paired results. Among 186 episodes with interpretable rifampicin and additional resistance results, 75 (40.3%) had resistance to at least one additional drug class, including 21/112 (18.8%) rifampicin-susceptible and 54/74 (73.0%) rifampicin-resistant episodes. Among 92 resistant episodes with complete profiles, 66 (71.7%) showed resistance to two or more drug classes. rpoB3- and rpoB4-associated signals predominated among rifampicin-resistant episodes, katG-associated signals among isoniazid-resistant episodes, and gyrA targets among fluoroquinolone-resistant episodes. Mixed wild-type and mutation-associated signals occurred across rpoB and gyrA. These findings support the use of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing as a component of regional drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance, enabling systematic characterization of multiclass resistance and molecular resistance patterns within routine diagnostic networks. Such molecular surveillance should be integrated with phenotypic susceptibility testing and genomic sequencing to resolve discordant, atypical, or clinically consequential profiles and build a more comprehensive regional resistance-monitoring system.

after.authors: Onoro-Morales, A. B.; Roy-Vallejo, E.; Pozo Ocampo, F.; Molina Montero, R.; Blancas Gomez-Casero, R.; Rodriguez-Serrano, D. A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Hospital Universitario Príncipe de Asturias; Universidad Alfonso X el Sabio
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Background: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) mortality remains high among patients with severe coronavirus disease. Static admission severity scores may fail to capture the dynamic clinical trajectory of critically ill patients. We hypothesized that early multiorgan failure (MOF) at 24 hours would improve mortality discrimination beyond admission severity alone. Methods: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 345 adults with severe COVID-19 pneumonia admitted to a Spanish ICU (March 2020-December 2022). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Univariate comparisons between survivors and non-survivors were performed, followed by multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of mortality. Three sequential models were constructed and compared by Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) discrimination. Results: Overall, in-hospital mortality was 20.6%. Non-survivors were older and had higher Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) II and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II scores (p<0.001). MOF at 24 hours was more frequent among non-survivors than survivors (88.4% vs. 61.7%, p<0.001). The baseline model (age, sex, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), hypertension, and SAPS II) achieved an AUC of 0.798 (95% CI 0.742-0.852). The final model incorporating MOF at 24 hours achieved an AUC of 0.812 (95% CI 0.754-0.860); early MOF nearly tripled the odds of death (OR 2.78, 95% CI 1.22-6.33, p=0.015). Conclusions: Combining baseline severity with early multiorgan dysfunction provides a simple, interpretable approach to mortality risk stratification in critically ill COVID-19 patients; however, external validation is needed before it can inform escalation-of-care or treatment-limitation decisions in clinical practice.

after.title: Preprint: Door-to-Valve Time and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Decompensated Severe Aortic Stenosis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
after.authors: Ma, J. R.; Gerges, M.; Koshy, A.; Wilson, W.; Taylor, A.; Chan, W.
after.abstract: Background: Acute decompensated aortic stenosis (ADAS) carries high mortality, but the optimal timing of valve intervention is unknown. Objective: To assess the association between time to valve intervention (transcatheter aortic valve replacement [TAVR] or balloon aortic valvuloplasty [BAV]) and clinical outcomes in ADAS. Methods: Embase, Ovid MEDLINE and CENTRAL were searched to May 15, 2026. Hazard ratios (HRs) for delayed versus earlier intervention were pooled using random-effects models with modified Hartung-Knapp inference. Unadjusted short-term mortality risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel method. Results: Eight observational cohort studies (n=6,044) met inclusion criteria: six TAVR (n= 5,986) and two BAV (n=58) studies. Patients were approximately 79 years old, and 63% were male. Early-intervention thresholds ranged from <24-48 hours (BAV) to ?22 days (TAVR) from admission. Delayed intervention was not significantly associated with long-term all-cause mortality (HR 1.52, 95% CI 0.46-5.00; p=0.269; I2=58.2%) or mortality per five-day delay (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.34-3.43; p=0.530; I2=86.7%). Crude short-term mortality was higher with delayed intervention (RR 4.96, 95% CI 1.17-20.92; p=0.029; I2=0.0%), although this association was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Most studies were at serious risk of bias, with substantial heterogeneity in clinical severity, intervention timing, and treatment modality. Conclusion: Point estimates favour earlier intervention, but current observational data do not establish a mortality benefit for an optimal door-to-valve interval, and existing study designs are biased against early treatment. Prospective and randomized-controlled trials on optimal valve intervention timing following ADAS are needed.

after.authors: Allende-Richter, S.; Stamoulis, C.; Reynier-Hernandez, A.; Brown, C. A.; Pollock, Z. E.; Chiert, H.; Gooding, H. C.; de Ferranti, S. D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Boston Children's Hospital Division of General Pediatrics
after.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among women, with risk factors commonly emerging during adolescence. Emerging evidence indicates that psychological factors, such as optimism, affect cardiovascular health, yet this remains understudied among young women. To assess the association between overall outlook on life and preventive cardiovascular health behaviors among young women. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of a cohort of 331 young women aged 15 to 24 years who completed the modified American Heart Association Women?s Health Survey (2017-2018), using multivariate regression adjusted for confounding. Results: Over 50% of young women felt their outlook on life may impact their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease. Outlook on life was associated with prioritizing and taking care of health (?=0.18-0.19, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.09, 0.29]; P=0.002) and usually following recommended healthy eating (?=0.12, 95% CI [0.03, 0.23]; P=0.016). Young women who identified as black (27.5%; N=91) felt that their outlook on life had a lower impact on their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease (Odds Ratio (OR)=0.80; 95% CI [0.65, 0.98]; P = 0.04), compared to other racial groups. Conclusion: Our findings support previous observations indicating a cardioprotective role of optimism in cardiovascular health. However, this association may not hold among young women of color, potentially reflecting constraints in their lived environment that limit how much a positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes. Strategies to reduce cardiovascular disease in women should address young women?s cardiovascular health and psychological and contextual factors, with particular attention to young women of color.

after.title: Preprint: Dynamic changes in plasma sphingosine-1-phosphate concentrations and mortality in sepsis: a prospective cohort study in the emergency department
after.authors: Tran, B. V.; Chen, C.-L.; Nguyen, T. N.; Lin, Y.-C.; Hu, K.-C.; Hsu, C.-W.; Hsu, S.-C.
after.abstract: Background Sepsis is a dynamic process with evolving host responses, biomarker changes, and organ dysfunction. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid involved in endothelial and immune regulation. However, the clinical relevance of dynamic S1P changes in sepsis remains unclear. This study aimed to assess their association with mortality. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study of adults recruited from the emergency department of Wan Fang Hospital between April 2022 and October 2024. Plasma S1P was measured by ELISA on days 1, 3, and before discharge or death. The primary outcome was 60-day mortality. S1P trajectories were defined by baseline concentrations and longitudinal slopes estimated using linear mixed-effects models. Low-decreasing, low-stable, and high-decreasing trajectories were grouped as descending; the others as ascending. Cox proportional hazards models assessed mortality associations with baseline S1P, trajectory groups, and time-varying S1P. Results Among 278 participants, 156 had sepsis. Baseline S1P concentrations were lower in patients with sepsis (82.2 [IQR, 47.8-141.1] ng/mL) than in those with non-septic infection (129.2 [IQR, 68.1-306.9] ng/mL) and non-infected controls (132.8 [IQR, 74.1-300.2] ng/mL). In the sepsis cohort, 101 patients were classified into the descending S1P trajectory group and 55 into the ascending group. The descending group had a higher hazard of 60-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 3.43; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11-10.58; p = 0.032). Baseline S1P was not significantly associated with 60-day mortality (aHR 1.004 per 10 ng/mL decrease; 95% CI, 0.977-1.032; p = 0.803). Each 10 ng/mL decrease in time-varying S1P was associated with a 3.5% higher mortality hazard (aHR 1.035; 95% CI, 1.002-1.076; p = 0.041). Conclusions Declining plasma S1P over time was associated with higher mortality in sepsis. Dynamic changes in S1P may be clinically relevant beyond baseline levels.

after.authors: Reynolds, K. M.; Lash, J.; Morris, A.; Daviglus, M. L.; Gallo, L. C.; Taylor, K. D.; Cai, J.; Cui, J.; Mattix-Kramer, H.; Chen, Y.-D. I.; Sotres-Alvarez, D.; Rotter, J. I. I.; Goodarzi, M. O.; Franceschini, N.

after.abstract: Increased fasting insulin reflects insulin resistance and is as a precursor to type 2 diabetes and a risk factor for kidney, heart and liver diseases and mortality. Cluster-specific fasting insulin polygenic scores (PS) characterize insulin resistance mechanisms based on insulin-related genetic associations with metabolic traits, and they have not been evaluated for liver outcomes. We calculated seven previously developed FI cluster-specific PS, including non-diabetogenic (Preserved Insulin Secretion, Elevated Insulin Secretion, Proinsulin) and diabetogenic clusters (Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia, Visceral Adiposity, Lipodystrophy, Liver/Lipid) in 12,631 participants of the Hispanic Community Healthy Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), and tested their association with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular, kidney and liver outcomes. We also tested the association of FI clusters with indices of insulin homeostasis in additional 1,316 Hispanic individuals. Among HCHS/SOL participants (mean age 46 years, 59% women, 20% with diabetes), we validated associations of FI cluster-specific PS and the 19 traits used to generate clusters. The Lipodystrophy cluster was associated with type 2 diabetes (p-value =3.5 x 10-5). In addition, the Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia cluster was associated with the hepatic steatosis index (p-value = 2.2 x1017) and the fatty liver index (p-value = 1.7 x1014), while the Liver/Lipid cluster with liver fibrosis (p-value = 1.5 x104) and lower kidney function (p-value = 5.2 x 10-5). The non-diabetogenic Elevated Insulin Secretion cluster-specific PS was associated with the disposition index (p = 0.0015). These results support insulin resistance mechanisms implicated in type 2 diabetes, liver and kidney outcomes.

after.authors: Rhead, R. D.; Hatch, S. L.; Das-Munshi, J.; Davis, S.; Dregan, A.; Ploubidis, G. B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychological Medicine, King's College London, London, UK; ESRC Centre for Society and Mental Health, King's College London, London, UK
after.abstract: Background In the UK, declining home ownership and delayed entry into the housing market have reshaped patterns of housing tenure (whether people own or rent their homes) across adulthood. Home ownership may reflect socioeconomic advantage, but may also provide greater housing security, stability and control, with implications for mental health. Using data from the 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70), this study examines how home ownership trajectories, defined by whether, when and for how long individuals own their homes, are associated with mental health in midlife. Methods We analysed data from 8,016 BCS70 participants with information on housing tenure histories and mental health outcomes at age 51. Housing tenure was measured repeatedly from ages 26 to 46 and used to define prespecified patterns of home ownership across adulthood (referred to as ownership regimes), including sustained ownership and never owning. Mental health outcomes at age 51 were psychological distress and positive mental wellbeing. G-estimation of a structural nested mean model was used to estimate contrasts between these ownership regimes while accounting for time-varying confounding affected by prior exposure. Models were estimated in lavaan; non-response weights and full information maximum likelihood were used to address selective attrition and missing data. Results At age 51, 71% of participants owned their home (23% outright and 48% with a mortgage), while 24% were renting and 5% lived in other arrangements. Sustained home ownership across adulthood was associated with lower psychological distress at age 51 compared with never owning (ATE -0.21, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.03) and higher positive mental wellbeing (ATE 0.56 SD, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.67). In ownership-history regime contrasts, late ownership (first ownership in one's 40s) was associated with lower psychological distress than never owning (ATE -0.15, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.04), while the estimate for early ownership (first ownership in one's 30s) was in the same direction but imprecise (ATE -0.12, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.04). For wellbeing, both late and early ownership were associated with higher scores than never owning (ATE 0.17 SD, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.27 and ATE 0.40 SD, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.51, respectively), with the largest association observed for sustained ownership. Conclusion Home ownership across adulthood (age 26 to 46) was associated with better mental health in midlife (age 51) after accounting for time-varying socio-economic and health-related confounding. Home ownership may reflect socioeconomic advantage, but may also provide greater housing security, stability and control, with implications for mental health. Using data from the 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70), this study examines how home ownership trajectories, defined by whether, when and for how long individuals own their homes, are associated with mental health in midlife. Methods We analysed data from 8,016 BCS70 participants with information on housing tenure histories and mental health outcomes at age 51. Housing tenure was measured repeatedly from ages 26 to 46 and used to define prespecified patterns of home ownership across adulthood (referred to as ownership regimes), including sustained ownership and never owning. Mental health outcomes at age 51 were psychological distress and positive mental wellbeing. G-estimation of a structural nested mean model was used to estimate contrasts between these ownership regimes while accounting for time-varying confounding affected by prior exposure. Models were estimated in lavaan; non-response weights and full information maximum likelihood were used to address selective attrition and missing data. Results At age 51, 71% of participants owned their home (23% outright and 48% with a mortgage), while 24% were renting and 5% lived in other arrangements. Sustained home ownership across adulthood was associated with lower psychological distress at age 51 compared with never owning (ATE -0.21, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.03) and higher positive mental wellbeing (ATE 0.56 SD, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.67). In ownership-history regime contrasts, late ownership (first ownership in one's 40s) was associated with lower psychological distress than never owning (ATE -0.15, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.04), while the estimate for early ownership (first ownership in one's 30s) was in the same direction but imprecise (ATE -0.12, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.04). For wellbeing, both late and early ownership were associated with higher scores than never owning (ATE 0.17 SD, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.27 and ATE 0.40 SD, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.51, respectively), with the largest association observed for sustained ownership. Conclusion Home ownership across adulthood (age 26 to 46) was associated with better mental health in midlife (age 51) after accounting for time-varying socio-economic and health-related confounding. Findings suggest that both the timing and persistence of ownership may matter, particularly for positive mental wellbeing, with more sustained exposure to ownership associated with more favourable outcomes.

after.authors: Srivathsan, A.; Navarro, M. A.; Arzika, A. M.; Abdou, A.; Maliki, R.; Ibrahim, A.; Beidi, D.; Galo, N.; Harouna, N.; Karamba, A. M.; Abarchi, M.; Peterson, B.; Ante-Testard, P. A.; Lebas, E.; Porco, T. C.; Lipsitch, M.; O'Brien, K. S.; Lietman, T. M.; Arnold, B. F.

after.abstract: Treatment effects in randomized trials may vary geographically, and estimating this variation is a broadly generalizable problem for large-scale, cluster-randomized trials. We conducted a secondary analysis of AVENIR, a cluster-randomized, placebo-controlled trial of biannual azithromycin distribution among children aged 1-59 months in Dosso, Niger (2020-2023). We assessed whether the survival benefit of mass azithromycin distribution varied geographically using Poisson models to estimate spatially continuous child mortality and average treatment effects (ATE). Among 1390 villages (276,452 person-years; 3635 deaths), the overall mortality rate was 13.1 and the ATE was -2.6 deaths per 1000 person-years. Mortality was highest in the south, whereas treatment benefit was concentrated in the southeast, following a northwest-southeast gradient. Aggregation of data to 160 primary health catchment areas preserved broad spatial patterns in mortality but attenuated local heterogeneity, suggesting that health catchment monitoring is sufficient for broad mortality surveillance. Examining unit-level, spatially predicted treatment effects as a function of mortality rate demonstrated that underlying mortality captured much, but not all, of the heterogeneity in treatment effects. The analysis demonstrates how to estimate localized treatment effects in large cluster-randomized trials and provides new insights into spatial heterogeneity in mortality and benefits of azithromycin distribution in Niger.

after.authors: McQuaid, G. A.; Tao, S.; Shea, L. L.; Wallace, G. L.
after.abstract: Objective: Contributors to autistic adults' elevated risk for negative aging-related outcomes, including Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), falls, and mortality remain underexplored. One candidate factor is exposure to medications with anticholinergic (AC) effects. Thus, this study assessed prevalence of medications with AC effects, and their associations with ADRD, falls, and mortality across four groups: autism-only, autism+intellectual disability (ID), ID-only, and controls. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2017-2019 US linked Medicare and Medicaid claims data for 40+ year-olds. Autism, ID, ADRD, and falls were identified using validated algorithms, and mortality was based on Medicare/Medicaid death indicators. Medications were coded using a comprehensive AC potency scale. AC medication exposure effects and interactions between AC potency and group were examined using modified Poisson regressions. Sensitivity analyses to address indication bias excluded persons prescribed antidepressant and/or antipsychotic medication(s). Results: All three clinical groups experienced significantly greater AC medication exposure (autism+ID: 92.5%>ID-only: 88.6%>autism-only: 80.0%) than non-autistic/non-ID controls (61.3%). Additionally, AC medications were more frequently associated with ADRD, falls, and mortality in all of these groups. Stepwise associations between AC potency levels and ADRD, falls, and mortality were found, and these effects were more prominent for persons with autism and/or ID relative to the control sample. Interpretation: This study provides a foundational examination of exposure to AC medication effects and their associations with aging-related outcomes in middle-age and older autistic adults and adults with ID. AC medication exposure represents one potential modifiable risk factor for negative aging-related outcomes in these groups.

after.authors: Jung, G.; Heo, Y.-R.; Hu, K.-S.; Kim, H.-J.
after.abstract: Objectives: To determine whether similar baseline discrimination conceals different responses to synthetic occlusion, whether loss of discrimination is accompanied by reduced confidence, and whether spatial attributions are reproducible in intraoral ultrasonography models. Methods: We analysed 477 images from 40 healthy volunteers, using acquisition position to label superior and inferior subregions. Five architectures were evaluated across five training seeds on a subject-independent test set of 97 images from eight volunteers. Images underwent constant-intensity occlusion at boundaries spanning 30-70% of image depth and an area-matched band-occlusion control. Attribution analyses assessed variation across seeds and class-activation methods and compared attribution-guided insertion with random insertion. Results: Seed-mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.958 to 0.972, with rankings reversing across seeds. EfficientNet-B0 fell below 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions, compared with zero to two for the other architectures; the difference persisted with area-matched masking. Under 50% occlusion, its mean confidence on incorrect predictions rose to 0.989 and expected calibration error from 0.094 to 0.478. Between two inference runs, EfficientNet-B0's per-seed occluded AUCs differed by up to 0.161; seed means were 0.51-0.55 in both. Attribution patterns varied across seeds and methods.

after.abstract: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI), a subtype of traumatic brain injury (TBI), can disrupt corticobulbar pathways, leading to chronic deficits in speech and swallowing. We present a first-in-human case study demonstrating the long-term therapeutic potential of low-frequency continuous deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the motor thalamus to restore corticobulbar function in a patient with severe DAI and persistent dysarthria and dysphagia. The patient underwent bilateral motor thalamus DBS implantation one-year post-injury for treatment of post-traumatic action tremor, and stimulation was delivered chronically at 55 Hz over three years of follow-up. We assessed orofacial motor outcomes using kinematic analysis of facial movements, videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, and speech tasks to dissociate the immediate assistive effects of stimulation (DBS ON versus OFF) from its long-term therapeutic effects (DBS OFF over time). Continuous DBS led to progressive recovery of facial symmetry, resolution of laryngeal penetration, and marked improvements in respiratory and phonatory control and speech intelligibility. While improvements in gross orofacial motor function persisted in the absence of stimulation, fine articulatory control remained dependent on ongoing stimulation or adjunct speech therapy for optimal performance. Stimulation-induced improvements in cervical posture may also have contributed to enhanced biomechanics of swallowing and voice production. These findings provide early evidence that low-frequency motor thalamus DBS may promote therapeutic benefits and extend the window of functional recovery in chronic TBI patients.

after.authors: Potter, A. W.; Murphy, C. E.; Wasfy, J. H.; Friedl, K. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Rutgers School of Health Professions Department of Health Informatics
after.abstract: Background: Body mass index (BMI) does not characterize central adiposity and may obscure cardiometabolic risk among adults classified as normal weight. We evaluated associations between waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) and incident disease across the BMI spectrum and among adults with normal BMI. Methods: We studied 308,600 adults in the All of Us Research Program. Participants with the corresponding prevalent disease were excluded separately for eight cardiometabolic outcomes. Cause-specific Cox models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, smoking, and BMI-related factors. We evaluated continuous and nonlinear WHtR associations, elevated WHtR among normal-BMI adults, and incremental discrimination. Additional analyses tested WHtR-by-BMI-category interactions. Results: Among 77,684 adults with normal BMI, 24,301 (31.3%) had WHtR 0.50. In whole-cohort analyses, adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) per 0.05 higher WHtR ranged from 1.07 to 1.31 across the eight outcomes. In BMI-stratified interaction models, corresponding diabetes HRs were 1.52 (95% CI, 1.43-1.61) in normal BMI, 1.42 (1.36-1.49) in overweight, and 1.22 (1.20-1.25) in obesity (P for interaction <0.001). Hypertension associations also differed across BMI groups (P for interaction <0.001). Among normal-BMI adults, WHtR 0.50 versus <0.50 was associated with diabetes (HR, 1.74), myocardial infarction (1.49), and ischemic stroke (1.52). Associations with all eight outcomes persisted in normal-BMI landmark analyses excluding the first year. Flexible age adjustment preserved the principal findings. Adding nonlinear WHtR improved cross-validated discrimination, most notably for diabetes (C-index=0.0134). Conclusions: WHtR identified cardiometabolic risk beyond BMI classification. Associations with diabetes and hypertension were particularly pronounced among normal-BMI adults, supporting assessment of central adiposity alongside BMI.

after.authors: Moratilla-Lapena, L.; Encinas, J. L.; Antolin, E.; Sanchez Torres, A.; Hernandez Oliveros, F.
after.abstract: Objective: O/E LHR is a well-established prenatal severity marker in congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), but its capacity to predict the postnatal need for delayed abdominal wall closure (DAC) remains undefined. We aimed to determine its predictive capacity. Method: Retrospective analysis of neonates with isolated left-sided CDH (2015-2026), comparing primary closure with DAC. Discriminative capacity was assessed by ROC analysis and the optimal cut-off was determined by bootstrap-aggregated approach. Logistic regression estimated univariate and liver herniation adjusted multivariate odds ratios (OR). Result: 45 neonates were included, 28 underwent primary closure and 17 required DAC. DAC was associated with lower gestational age, higher rates of liver herniation, greater ECMO requirement, and higher mortality than primary closure (all p < 0.01). O/E LHR showed excellent discriminative ability for DAC (AUC 0.939), with an optimal cut-off of 34.1% (sensitivity 82.35%, specificity 82.14%, positive predictive value 73.68%, negative predictive value 88.46%). O/E LHR was independently associated with DAC after multivariate analysis (OR 0.821, 95% CI 0.668-0.939, p = 0.002). Conclusions: O/E LHR was independently associated with DAC risk beyond liver herniation. These preliminary findings suggest a potential role for O/E LHR in prenatal risk stratification for DAC, pending external validation.

after.title: Preprint: The Feasibility, Acceptability, and Perceived Need for Suicide Initiatives for Children in UK Primary Schools
after.authors: Abdul Salam, B.; Saini, P.; McCarthy, M.; Smith, N.; Ashworth, E.
after.abstract: Abstract Background: Currently, there are no specific suicide prevention programmes for primary (elementary) schools within the UK. However, given the rise in suicidal thoughts and/or behaviours amongst children under 11 years, the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived need for these programmes need to be assessed.  Aims: This qualitative scoping study aimed to explore whether there is a perceived need for suicide prevention programmes in primary schools and, if so, what these should look like. Sample(s) & Methods: 92 participants took part in the study. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with mental health professionals (N= 22), school staff (N= 8), and parents of children who had experienced suicidal ideation, behaviours, or been bereaved by suicide (N=7). Focus groups were conducted with secondary school students (N= 36) and primary school students (N= 19) across 5 schools. Data were analysed using thematic framework analysis.   Results: Three main themes were identified: 1) the necessity of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, 2) barriers affecting delivery and potential solutions, 3) the transition period from primary to secondary school. Conclusion: Overall, participants supported the need and acceptability of suicide prevention programmes for primary schools, particularly due to the rising concerns about suicidality among younger children and evidence that suicide-related discussions are already occurring within peer groups. However, careful consideration needs to be given to ensure it is delivered in a safe and age-appropriate way, with a focus on dispelling myths, promoting help seeking, and increasing knowledge.

after.authors: Mbogning Fonkou, M. D.
after.abstract: Introduction. Between 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHO's 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. Methods. I analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. Results. Women held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). Conclusions. Before the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field.

after.title: Preprint: Estimated impacts of mandatory sodium reformulation targets on sodium consumption, health outcomes, health sector costs and health equity in Aotearoa New Zealand
after.authors: Fuavao, K.; Cleghorn, C.; McKenzie, B.; Widyastuti, N.; McLean, R.; Swinburn, B.; Ni Mhurchu, C.; Nosa, V.; Eyles, H.
after.abstract: Aims Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ), including for M[a]ori, the Indigenous population. Sodium intake is a modifiable CVD risk factor. In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) released sodium reduction benchmarks for 58 packaged food categories. We aimed to estimate the health, health-sector cost, and equity impacts of mandating these benchmarks in NZ. Methods Nationally representative data on household food purchases, packaged food sodium content, and dietary intake were used to estimate baseline sodium consumption (2011) and changes following implementation of the WHO benchmarks. A dietary multi-state life-table model estimated impacts on health-adjusted life years (HALYs) and health system costs (2011 NZ$, 3% discount rate) over the remaining lifetime of the 2011 NZ population (n = 4.4 million). Analyses examined impacts by sex and for M[a]ori. Results Mandatory reformulation was estimated to reduce sodium intake by 470 mg/day per person (1.18 g salt), a 22% reduction from baseline. Across population groups, age-standardised reductions ranged from 380 to 660 mg/day (22-23%), generating an estimated 55,600 HALYs (95% uncertainty interval 19,100-90,000) and NZ$535.2 million in health-system cost savings (95% UI: 183.0-914.6 million) over the population lifetime. M[a]ori gained 11,600 HALYs (95% UI: 4,900-17,700), equivalent to 17.2 HALYs per 1,000 population, compared with 11.8 per 1,000 among non-M[a]ori. Conclusion Mandating WHO sodium benchmarks in NZ could substantially reduce sodium intake, improve population health, reduce health sector costs, and advance health equity. Findings support adoption of this strategy in Aotearoa NZ.

after.title: Preprint: The Para-ISS Dural Space Enhancement Sign: A Novel MRI Finding Independently Associated With Intracranial Atherosclerotic Burden
after.authors: Zeng, S.; Lin, D.; Tang, K.; Zeng, F.; Zheng, X.; Li, M.; Lin, J.; Huang, B.; Zhan, S.; Chen, S.; Dai, Z.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Radiology, Shantou Central Hospital, Shantou 515031, China; Clinical Research Center, Shantou Central Hospital, Shantou 515031, China
after.abstract: Background: No dural enhancement sign centered on the inferior sagittal sinus (ISS) has been characterized. We observed a frequent, previously undescribed finding - para-ISS dural space enhancement (PISE) - at the free inferior margin of the falx cerebri. Objective: To define PISE, determine its detection rate in a large cross-sectional cohort, and characterize its correlates, in particular whether the pattern of association is compatible with an atherosclerosis-related dural mechanism. Methods: Consecutive contrast-enhanced intracranial vessel-wall MRI (VWI) examinations (May 2015-December 2025) were reviewed; 835 of 875 examinations were evaluable, corresponding to 811 patients. The first outcome-evaluable examination for each patient was used for all primary analyses. PISE was defined as dural enhancement strictly at the falx free margin adjacent to the ISS, exceeding the ISS vascular lumen. Forty-seven demographic, clinical-history, and imaging variables were tested univariately with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; multivariable logistic regression with patient-grouped 5-fold cross-validation was triangulated with LASSO and random forest. Dose-response across plaque grades was assessed with the Cochran-Armitage trend test, and circulation-specific associations were compared in models adjusted for age and sex (inter-reader Cohen's kappa = 0.93). Results: PISE was detected in 609/811 patients (75.1%); detection rose from 50.0% (<40 years) to 81.7% (>70 years; trend p = 5.6 x 10^-6). The strongest univariate correlate was vulnerable intracranial plaque (OR=8.29, 95% CI 5.54-12.40). Detection increased across plaque grades 0/1/2 (38.7% -> 77.2% -> 90.3%; Z=11.09). Anterior-circulation plaque showed a stronger association than posterior-circulation plaque (OR=4.42 vs 2.76). Vulnerable plaque (OR=2.37), plaque grade (OR=2.84 per grade), age (OR=1.38 per SD), and inpatient status (OR=3.18) remained independently associated (patient-grouped cross-validated AUC=0.755). Moyamoya disease was inversely associated (OR=0.25). Findings were consistent across imputation and all-examination sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: PISE is a frequently detected novel dural enhancement sign whose independent, graded, anatomically concordant association with intracranial atherosclerotic burden supports an atherosclerosis-related dural mechanism and warrants prospective validation.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Prediction of elective surgical red blood cell transfusion reveals surgeon-level variation

after.title: Preprint: Prediction of elective surgical red blood cell transfusion reveals surgeon-level variation
after.authors: Turkulainen, E.; Arvas, M.; Koskinen, M.; Ilmakunnas, M.
after.abstract: BACKGROUND Preoperative prediction of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in elective surgery serves two complementary purposes: enabling patient blood management (PBM) interventions before surgery and supporting blood product supply planning for elective lists. Beyond patient risk factors, individual surgeon practice may also contribute to transfusion rates, but this effect has not been fully quantified. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS In a retrospective cohort of 279,905 elective surgical procedures at Helsinki University Hospital (2021-2025), we trained four gradient-boosted tree (CatBoost) models crossing patient factors with procedure group and pseudonymised surgeon identity. All predictors were restricted to data available seven or more days before scheduled surgery. The primary outcome was any allogeneic RBC transfusion from operating-room entry through seven postoperative days. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on a held-out 20% test set. Surgeon-level effects were characterised by Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values. RESULTS The transfusion rate was 2.2%. The patient-only model achieved AUPRC 0.261 (no-skill baseline 0.022). Adding surgeon identity to the procedure-adjusted model increased AUPRC from 0.440 to 0.472 (+0.032; 95% CI 0.020-0.044), raising lift from 20.3 to 21.7. Surgeon identity was the third most important of 72 features by permutation importance. DISCUSSION The operating surgeon was associated with RBC transfusion beyond patient and procedure factors, and surgeon identity was the third most important predictor in a deployment-realistic model using only data available a week before surgery. This information is readily available from routine records and could support PBM audit and blood supply planning for elective surgery.

after.title: Preprint: Diagnostic Value in Discarded Reads: Re-evaluating Multi-Mapping cfDNA Fragmentomics and GC Bias in Early-Stage Cancer.
after.authors: Kadali, N.; UPPALURI, K. R.; Challa, H. J.; Vempati, K. K.
after.abstract: Background. Low-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. Methods. We analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I to III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. Results. The multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95 % CI 0.67 - 0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64 - 0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71 - 0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62 - 1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. Conclusions. Multi-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.

after.title: Preprint: Single-Cell Transcriptome-Wide Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analysis Reveals Immune Cell-Specific Mechanisms in Alzheimer's Disease
after.authors: Si, Y.; Si, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Human Anatomy, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou 450001, Henan, China
after.abstract: Objective: To integrate single-cell expression quantitative trait locus (sc-eQTL), Alzheimer's disease (AD) genome-wide association study (GWAS), and Bayesian colocalization analyses, in order to systematically identify candidate causal genes and potential immune mechanisms that specifically regulate AD risk in peripheral immune cells. Methods: Using the cis-eQTLs of 14 peripheral blood immune cell types from the OneK1K single-cell eQTL dataset as exposure data and the AD GWAS (GCST90565439) as outcome data, a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was performed. Weak instrumental variables were removed using F-statistics, and approximately independent genetic instruments were obtained by linkage disequilibrium pruning. For significant gene-cell type associations, compareCluster functional enrichment, Bayesian colocalization, and phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) were further performed, and the 1M-scBloodNL dataset was used for replication validation. Results: The MR analysis identified 187 gene-cell type associations significantly associated with AD risk, involving 161 candidate causal genes. Among them, 141 genes showed significant associations in only a single immune cell type, suggesting that AD-related immune genetic regulation has marked cell type specificity. Functional enrichment analysis showed that the significant genes in different immune cell types were enriched in biological processes including MHC class II antigen presentation, phagocytosis, membrane invagination, and positive regulation of T cell activation. Colocalization analysis indicated a strong shared genetic signal between TNF expression in CD4+SOX4+ T cells and AD risk (PP.H4 = 0.833). In the 1M-scBloodNL replication analysis, several candidate genes showed consistent direction and nominal significance. The PheWAS results suggested that the significant phenotypic associations of the TNF instrumental variable were mainly concentrated in immune- and hematology-related traits, with no genome-wide significant neurological phenotypic associations observed. Conclusion: This study suggests that single-cell eQTL-MR combined with colocalization analysis can be used to dissect the cell type-specific genetic regulatory mechanisms of peripheral immunity in AD. The genetically predicted expression of TNF in CD4+SOX4+ T cells may represent an important immune-related signal for AD risk, but further validation in independent populations and functional experiments is still required.

The PheWAS results suggested that the significant phenotypic associations of the TNF instrumental variable were mainly concentrated in immune- and hematology-related traits, with no genome-wide significant neurological phenotypic associations observed. Conclusion: This study suggests that single-cell eQTL-MR combined with colocalization analysis can be used to dissect the cell type-specific genetic regulatory mechanisms of peripheral immunity in AD. The genetically predicted expression of TNF in CD4+SOX4+ T cells may represent an important immune-related signal for AD risk, but further validation in independent populations and functional experiments is still required.

after.title: Preprint: Deep learning screening of otoscopic images for ENT referral: development, validation and deployment of NHREF OtoScan
after.authors: MUNAWEERA THANTREEGE, D. L.; Chandrasena, L. G.; De Mel, V.; Gautham, B. K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Nawaloka Hospitals Research and Education Foundation
after.abstract: Background. Middle and external ear disease is common and largely treatable, but accurate otoscopic interpretation requires training that is scarce outside specialist ENT services. Published deep learning models for otoscopy report high accuracy, yet most are optimised for closed set classification rather than the referral decision a non specialist actually makes, report uncalibrated probabilities, and do not report the near duplicate controls that video derived otoscopic datasets demand. We developed, validated and deployed a screening aid framed around referral rather than diagnosis. Methods. We merged 4,763 otoscopic images from 16 folders across three public datasets into 12 clinically meaningful classes. Every image was passed through a single field of view normalisation function (crop to the illuminated field, square, resize to 224 px, mask to one fixed circle) shared identically by training and inference, to remove the framing cue that otherwise identifies the source dataset. Because one source is video derived, images were grouped by cosine similarity of generic ImageNet features (threshold 0.93, joined transitively) and whole groups assigned to a single split, giving 3,326 training, 719 validation and 718 test images. A MobileNetV2 backbone initialised from ImageNet was fine tuned from block9expand. Probabilities were averaged over the eight dihedral transforms of each image and temperature scaled. The referral score was one minus the probability of a normal ear, and its threshold was set on the validation abnormal ears as the highest value still meeting a target sensitivity of 97%, applied with an inclusive comparison. Model selection, calibration and threshold were frozen before the test split was scored once. Results. On the 718 held out test images, referral sensitivity was 97.0% (95% CI 95.1 to 98.2) and specificity 75.6% (95% CI 69.4 to 80.8), with AUROC 0.974 for abnormal versus normal; a cluster bootstrap over the 363 similarity groups in the test split widens those intervals to 93.8 99.6% and 66.0 83.4% respectively. Of 501 abnormal ears, 15 were not referred; 11 of these were myringosclerosis and none was cholesteatoma. Twelve class macro F1 was 0.686, balanced accuracy 68.3%, and accuracy 85.0% (86.2% with chronic subtypes merged). Temperature scaling (T = 1.2) reduced expected calibration error from 0.0498 to 0.0430. A low confidence flag fired on 4.0% of test images, separating 87.2% accuracy on unflagged from 31.0% on flagged cases. Recall was consistently highest on the largest source dataset and fell on the other two, for example acute otitis media 95.5% on source A versus 50.0% on source B. Conclusions. A compact, calibrated model run on ordinary CPU hardware achieved the pre specified 97% referral sensitivity with clinically interpretable failure modes. The source stratified gap, and an earlier perceptual hash split that inflated scores until it was corrected, indicate that headline accuracy in this field is strongly dependent on leakage control and acquisition style. The system is deployed with mandatory specialist review, a daily backtest and approval gated retraining, so that prospective performance on local equipment is measured rather than assumed. It is research software and not a medical device.

after.title: Preprint: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
after.authors: Dalal, A. K.; Lundstedt, J.; Ernecoff, N.; Plombon, S.; Streiter, S.; Leeson, M.; Plasek, J.; Mueller, S.; Fiskio, J.; Zhou, L.; Lipsitz, S.; Orkaby, A.; Loewenthal, J.
after.abstract: Background: Electronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from structured electronic health record (EHR) data may incompletely capture functional deficits. Large language models (LLMs) can extract frailty-related information from clinical notes, but whether improved frailty ascertainment improves prognostic performance is uncertain. Objective: To compare frailty ascertainment and prognostic performance between standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs among hospitalized adults. Design: Retrospective cohort study Participants: Adults aged 50 years or older enrolled in two studies at an academic medical center and affiliated community hospital between February 2022 and April 2024. Main Measures: A validated 35-deficit diagnosis-based eFI and an LLM-enhanced eFI incorporating deficits extracted from physical therapy (PT) documentation using GPT-4o. Frailty was defined using an index threshold of 0.20 or more. The primary outcome was a composite of discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations with the outcome, and discrimination was compared using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary analyses examined threshold-based classification and PT-documentation availability; prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated population and outcome restrictions. Results: Among 616 hospitalizations, mean (SD) age was 70.9 (10.2) years, 329 (53.4%) had PT documentation, and 320 (51.9%) experienced the composite outcome. Standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs classified 216 (35.1%) and 362 (58.8%) hospitalizations as frail, respectively. Both were independently associated with the outcome (standard eFI: adjusted OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.39-2.83]; LLM-enhanced eFI: adjusted OR, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.75-3.47]). Discrimination did not differ significantly (AUROC, 0.636 vs 0.660; difference, 0.024 [95% CI, -0.006 to 0.053]; p=0.12). LLM enhancement increased sensitivity (42.5% to 69.4%) but decreased specificity (73.0% to 52.7%). Conclusions: LLM enhancement substantially increased frailty ascertainment and sensitivity for adverse outcomes but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination. Thus, LLM-enhanced frailty assessment may depend on whether the intended use prioritizes broad identification of functional vulnerability or prediction of adverse post-hospital outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Syndemic burden, menopause, and cardiovascular risk among midlife and older women with and without HIV
after.authors: Pan, Y.; Cherenack, E. M.; Feaster, D. J.; Lu, Y.; Young, B.; McNeely, K. V.; Wilson, T.; Peters, B. A.; Levitan, E. B.; Moran, C.; Ramirez, C.; Topper, E. F.; Weber, K.; Abelman, R.; Spence, A. B.; Sternberg, C. A.; Fonseca Nogueira, N.; Martinez, C. A.; Alcaide, M. L.; Jones, D. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine
after.abstract: Midlife and older women living with HIV often carry several co-occurring social and behavioral stressors, and how that accumulated burden relates to cardiovascular risk is not well described. We examined whether cumulative syndemic burden was associated with estimated 10-year risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease among women aged 45 years and older, and whether menopause stage modified it. Data came from the MACS/WIHS Combined Cohort Study, a multisite United States cohort, for visits between October 2020 and March 2025. The full sample included 1,993 women, 1,446 of them living with HIV; a secondary sample of 1,063 women virally suppressed at baseline contributed 4,009 visits. Syndemic burden was the sum of six conditions: elevated depressive symptoms, current tobacco use, hazardous alcohol use, recent stimulant use, physical inactivity, and material insecurity. Ten-year cardiovascular risk was estimated with the Pooled Cohort Equations and modeled with linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts; random forest classifiers were trained separately to predict high estimated risk (7.5 percent or greater). Median age was 56 years, 63 percent were non-Hispanic Black, and 57 percent reported two or more syndemic conditions. Each additional syndemic condition was associated with a 0.40-point higher estimated risk score (95 percent confidence interval 0.01 to 0.78; p=0.043), and postmenopausal status with a 1.3-point higher score than premenopause (0.39 to 2.3; p=0.006). The syndemic burden by menopause stage interaction was not significant overall (p=0.2), although an exploratory signal was present among virally suppressed women (0.50; p=0.079). The classifiers discriminated moderately (areas under the curve 0.727 and 0.704); serum creatinine, body mass index, syndemic burden, and postmenopausal status ranked among the most important predictors. Syndemic burden and reproductive aging were each independently and modestly associated with higher estimated cardiovascular risk, supporting joint assessment of both in risk stratification for midlife women with and without HIV.

after.authors: Harris, A. W.; Thomas, A.; Ouedraogo, J.-B.; Tinto, H.; Zongo, I.; Dicko, A.; Sagara, I.; Chandramohan, D.; Greenwood, B.; Kurtovic, L.; Beeson, J.
after.abstract: The RTS,S vaccine provides moderate protection against malaria in children, which may be due in part to environmental factors. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infections are prevalent in Africa and potentially contribute to suboptimal vaccine responses. We evaluated whether latent CMV/EBV infections impact RTS,S-induced antibodies in 314 vaccinated children aged 5-29 months in West Africa. While no strong associations were observed for CMV, children seropositive for EBV had lower antigen-specific IgG and IgA, which have been linked with protective malaria immunity. These results may partly explain why malaria vaccines are suboptimal in populations where early CMV/EBV infections are prevalent.

after.authors: Jolliffe, D. A.; Middelkoop, K.; Ganmaa, D.; Irmuun, B.; Sluyter, J. D.; Sudfeld, C. R.; Fawzi, W. W.; Martineau, A. R.
after.abstract: Background: Several randomised controlled trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection and disease have been conducted, but no individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis has been conducted. Methods: We conducted a systematic review, one-stage and two-stage IPD meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420251173446) of double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection or disease. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to October 29, 2026. The co-primary outcomes were incident tuberculosis infection (evidenced by tuberculin skin test or Interferon Gamma Release Assay conversion) and incident tuberculosis disease. Mixed-effects models estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs), accounting for trial and prespecified covariates. Prespecified subgroup analyses investigated effect modification by sex and age, body-mass index, vitamin D status, and BCG vaccination status. Findings: Four trials contributed IPD for 14,619 participants. Vitamin D did not reduce risk of incident tuberculosis infection (9,557 participants; aOR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.18; p=0.79) or incident tuberculosis disease (14,533 participants; aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.10; p=0.15). There was no evidence of effect modification by participant characteristics investigated in sub-group analyses, including in participants with 25-hydroxyvitamin D <25 nmol/L (infection: aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.67-1.34; disease: 1.01, 0.45-2.30). Serious adverse events and mortality were unaffected. Interpretation: Vitamin D supplementation did not reduce the risk of incident tuberculosis infection or disease in the populations studied, either overall or within sub-groups. The 95% confidence interval of the effect estimate for prevention of tuberculosis disease remains compatible with a potentially important benefit, and further trials for this indication may be warranted. Funding: Barts Charity (ref G-002700).

after.authors: Suh, K.; Wang, S.; Donadee, C.; Boeltz, A.; Barbash, I. J.; Guo, X.; Alam, S.; Horvat, C.; Collier, V.; Rivosecchi, R.
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Background: Vasopressin is a commonly used adjunctive therapy in the management of septic shock. While vasopressin may provide clinical benefits, at times its acquisition cost has risen to being substantially more expensive than other second-line vasopressors such as epinephrine, phenylephrine, or dopamine. Additionally, mortality prediction tools such as the Global Open-Source Severity of Illness Score (GOSSIS) have emerged as a valuable resource to guide resource allocation in critical care. This study aimed to evaluate the healthcare costs associated with vasopressin use and assess the predictive performance of GOSSIS in patients with septic shock. Methods: We conducted a multi-center retrospective cohort study of adult ICU patients with septic shock treated throughout the UPMC Health System from January 2021 to January 2022. Patients who received norepinephrine as a first-line vasopressor followed by either vasopressin or an alternative vasopressor were included. Generalized linear models with a log link and gamma distribution were used to compare adjusted total healthcare costs. Recycled predictions were used to estimate marginal cost differences. GOSSIS performance was evaluated by comparing predicted versus observed ICU mortality across risk groups. Results: Among 3,898 eligible patients, 1,060 received vasopressin and 2,838 received alternative second-line vasopressors. Vasopressin use was associated with significantly higher adjusted hospital costs (cost ratio = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.08, 1.20). The estimated marginal cost difference was $5,887 per patient. Drug costs accounted for a greater proportion of total hospitalization costs among vasopressin users (20% vs. 12%). GOSSIS demonstrated strong calibration, with predicted ICU mortality closely aligning with observed rates across all severity strata. Conclusions: Vasopressin use in septic shock was associated with a 14% increase in hospitalization costs compared to alternative second-line vasopressors. The GOSSIS demonstrated strong predictive validity for ICU mortality, supporting its potential use in guiding resource allocation decisions in critically ill populations.

We aimed to identify clinically distinct phenotypes of early-onset heart failure in women, assess their prognostic significance, and evaluate their transportability in an independent national cohort. after.abstract: Abstract Background: Oral anticoagulation (OAC) reduces stroke risk in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), and screening can enable earlier AF detection and OAC initiation. However, the population-level trade-off between stroke prevention and OAC-related major bleeding for different types of AF and OAC therapy remains uncertain, and large randomized trials to resolve this are costly and time-consuming. Methods: A state-transition Markov-like model was developed to: 1) simulate the lifetime course of AF, stroke, major bleeding, and death in different virtual populations; 2) quantify benefits (stroke reduction) and harms (major bleeding) of systematic AF screening with screening-triggered OAC across CHA2DS2-VA scores; and 3) compare rhythm-guided, time-delimited ("pill-in-pocket") OAC with continuous OAC. Results: The model synthesized information from multiple clinical sources and reproduced stroke and bleeding incidence across clinical scenarios. At CHA?DS?-VA=2, long-term continuous rhythm monitoring (LT-CRM) with OAC lowered stroke risk (HR, 0.92 [95%CI, 0.88-0.96]) but raised bleeding risk (HR, 1.17 [95%CI, 1.07-1.27]) versus no screening. Time-to-benefit was shorter than time-to-harm for CHA?DS?-VA?4, but longer for CHA?DS?-VA=0. Pill-in-pocket OAC vs continuous OAC showed no difference in stroke/mortality (HR, 1.03, 95%CI [0.91-1.16]) but lower bleeding risk (HR, 0.81, 95%CI: 0.68-0.96]) in patients with elevated bleeding risk, but not at baseline. Sensitivity analyses revealed that the risk-benefit profiles of screening or pill-in-pocket OAC strategy further depend on OAC adherence and bleeding risks. Conclusions: Our model highlights a trade-off between stroke reduction and bleeding for systematic screening-initiated OAC, with net benefit for CHA?DS?-VA?4. We provide the first virtual implementation of an ongoing rhythm-guided OAC trial, showing that pill-in-pocket OAC may lower bleeding risk compared to continuous OAC, highlighting the potential of virtual clinical trials to guide clinical trial design.
