after.abstract: Background: Genetic abnormalities contribute to the phenotypic heterogeneity of congenital heart disease, yet their prognostic significance in adults with congenital heart disease remains incompletely understood. We examined the associations of pathogenic sequence variants and copy number variants (CNVs) with cardiovascular and major clinical outcomes in ACHD. Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, 1,000 adults with structurally confirmed CHD were recruited from a tertiary care center in Noida, India, between January 2022 and January 2026 and followed through August 2026. Participants underwent exome sequencing and chromosomal microarray analysis and were classified into four mutually exclusive groups: reference, sequence-variant-only, CNV-only, and dual-positive. The primary outcome was time to first occurrence of a composite of cardiovascular death, unplanned heart failure hospitalization, resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, heart transplantation, or durable mechanical circulatory support. Associations were evaluated using multivariable Cox regression. Results: Of 1,000 participants, 800 comprised the reference group, 120 had sequence variants only, 60 had CNVs only, and 20 had both sequence variants and CNVs. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 12.0%, 20.0%, 25.0%, and 30.0% of participants, respectively. In fully adjusted analyses, the sequence-variant-only group had a higher risk of the primary outcome versus the reference group (hazard ratio [HR], 1.65; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01?2.69; p=0.0455). The CNV-only group had an HR of 1.92 (95% CI, 1.04?3.52; p=0.0360). Neither association remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p=0.072 for both). The dual-positive group had an HR of 2.12 (95% CI, 0.83?5.42; p=0.1182). Extracardiac congenital anomalies and neurological disorders were more prevalent among individuals with genetic variants, while secondary outcomes showed no significant associations. Conclusions: Pathogenic sequence variants and CNVs were associated with numerically higher risks of adverse cardiovascular outcomes in ACHD, but independent prognostic significance was not established after adjustment for multiple testing.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Lebanese American University Gilbert and Rose-Marie Chagoury School of Medicine
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with excess mortality, and 2 randomized trials have tested early transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). OBJECTIVES: The authors sought to estimate the effects of early TAVR vs clinical surveillance and to compare randomized with observational estimates. METHODS: Six databases and registries were searched through November 3, 2026. Adjusted observational studies were synthesized separately from trials. Certainty was rated with GRADE. RESULTS: Two trials (922 patients; TAVR UNLOAD, n = 178, HF with reduced ejection fraction; PROGRESS, n = 744, 96.4% symptomatic) and 7 cohorts were included. Early TAVR did not detectably change death over approximately 2 years (HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.74-1.49; low certainty), with one-fifth of the deaths needed to detect a 20% reduction. Heart failure (HF) hospitalization was lower (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.36-0.77; low certainty), or 70 fewer patients per 1,000 at 2 years. New pacemakers were more frequent (PROGRESS: 17.3% vs 9.3%; moderate certainty). About half of surveillance patients underwent valve replacement within 2 years. Observational cohorts estimated a 48% mortality reduction (HR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.43-0.64; very low certainty), which differed from the randomized estimate (ratio of HRs: 2.01; 95% CI: 1.37-2.95). CONCLUSIONS: In older, predominantly symptomatic patients with moderate AS, early TAVR may make little or no difference to 2-year mortality and may reduce HF hospitalization, at the cost of more pacemakers. Because about half of patients under surveillance receive a valve within 2 years, the decision largely concerns timing. Observational survival estimates should not guide practice.

after.authors: Trauer, J. M.; Shipman, D. S.; Ryan, M.; Henderson, A. S.; McBryde, E. S.; Meehan, M. T.; Ragonnet, R.
after.abstract: COVID-19 provides an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate the contribution of public health and social measures (PHSMs) to controlling transmission and inform responses to future emerging respiratory pathogens. We analysed SARS-CoV-2 transmission across 126 countries spanning multiple epidemic waves and diverse policy environments during periods when PHSMs were the primary interventions available to influence the epidemic. By explicitly representing key epidemiological drivers of transmission and measuring reductions in residual transmission scaling after incorporating OxCGRT policy time-series data, we isolated the effect of PHSMs on transmission. PHSMs frequently explained a substantial proportion of the observed variation in transmission intensity, with particularly strong effects seen in many high-income countries. In countries with strong evidence for policy effects, reductions in transmission reached 60-80% or above, although the individual policies responsible for these effects varied considerably. Harmonised analyses considering the effect of community mobility showed comparably strong effects in a similar subset of countries.

after.abstract: Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly delivering chronic care in resource-constrained settings but require support to manage complex longitudinal clinical workflows. In the Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project in rural Lesotho, CHWs provide longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care, supported by the ComBaCaL Community Health Toolkit (CHT) application. The application combines longitudinal participant management and task coordination with clinical decision support for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, and follow-up for hypertension and diabetes care. This model of care has demonstrated improved or maintained clinical outcomes compared to facility-based care only. We conducted a mixed-methods study among all 103 participating CHWs to evaluate their experiences with the application. All CHWs completed a 38-item questionnaire, and 22 participated in qualitative interviews or focus group discussions. Overall usability was high, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 75.6 (SD 13.0), and 98 (95%) CHWs were satisfied or very satisfied with the application. General application functions and diagnosis and treatment tasks were rated easy or very easy by 98% of participants. The most frequently reported benefits were task reminders (92%), structured clinical guidance (87%), overview of allocated participants (81%), and retention of participant information (81%). Main challenges were lengthy questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, and limited internet connectivity. Qualitative findings showed that ease of use increased with experience, supported by training and supervision. Participants described how algorithmic guidance and task reminders supported care delivery, while also identifying tensions between standardized workflows and flexibility in day-to-day care. The ComBaCaL CHT application was highly usable and valued by CHWs. High perceived usability extended from general application functions to complex clinical workflows. CHT demonstrated suitability as a configurable framework for implementing such context-specific workflows for hypertension and diabetes care when accompanied by appropriate workflow design, training, and supervision.

after.abstract: Background Multiple viruses can cause acute respiratory infections (ARI), impacting morbidity, mortality and hospital resources. The objective of this study was to describe viral circulation among patients with ARI, patients characteristics and severity outcomes. Methods A retrospective cohort was assembled using electronic health records from the Hospices Civils de Lyon, France. Adult patients ([≥]18 years) hospitalised or presenting to the emergency department from October 2016 to April 2025 with either an ICD-10 diagnostic code for ARI or a laboratory-confirmed viral detection were included. Administrative variables and laboratory results collected during the stay were extracted. Results 103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 patients were included. The number of eligible stays increased substantially since the COVID-19 pandemic, along with year-round laboratory testing. Following disruption during the pandemic, winter peaks of ARI incidence, influenza and RSV detections re-emerged after 2022. Influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged [≥]80 years. Patients aged [≥]65 years had longer hospitalisations (median 10 vs 8 days, p<0.001), twice in-hospital mortality rate (14% vs 7%, p<0.001), less frequent ICU admission (21% vs 33%, p<0.001) and use of respiratory support than younger adults. Influenza was the virus associated with the shortest length of stays, hMPV was associated with the longest in younger adults. Conclusions Real-world hospital data are valuable for surveillance of viral circulation, early identification of patients at risk of deterioration, and may be used to evaluate the impact of preventive intervention in community.

However, this coincided with regional and national increases in SARS-CoV-2 detection in wastewater, suggesting ongoing community burden. Wide confidence intervals, lack of quantitative data, and limited data collection after the matches limit our conclusions. This study demonstrates the use of qualitative, multiplexed PCR assays for WBS during a mass gathering sporting event.

after.authors: Tampubolon, G.
after.abstract: Later-life quality of life is increasingly recognised as a life-course achievement, yet ageing research has focused more on dysfunction and decline than on positive wellbeing. This study examines whether childhood poverty shapes later-life quality of life, measured by CASP: control, autonomy, self-realisation and pleasure. METHODS: I analysed harmonised data from 59,569 adults aged over 50 in 29 countries, drawn from HRS, ELSA, SHARE and TILDA (U.S. Health and Retirement Study, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing). Childhood poverty was modelled as a latent class from retrospectively reported childhood material circumstances, acknowledging recall error in such reports. Country fixed-effects linear models estimated associations with CASP, first adjusting for age, sex and country, then adding education, marital status and later-life wealth. RESULTS: One in five participants grew up in poverty (22.9%). Mean CASP was 38 out of 48. Initially childhood poverty was associated with a 1.2-point lower CASP score; after complete adjustment the penalty attenuated but remained durable at 0.7 points. Education, partnership and wealth were independently associated with higher wellbeing but did not erase the penalty. Predicted age profiles showed poverty penalty in every country. They also revealed striking national differences: Nordic countries achieved markedly higher CASP levels than several Eastern European countries; Finns aged 90 had similar levels of positive wellbeing to Latvians two decades younger. CONCLUSION: Childhood poverty leaves a durable mark on later-life positive wellbeing, while welfare contexts appear to lift overall CASP levels. Reducing child poverty and strengthening social protection are therefore lifelong wellbeing policies.

after.abstract: Objective: To develop and psychometrically evaluate two new brief assessments measuring disease severity (the Severity of ME Scale, SoMES) and occupational status (the ME Occupational Status Scale, MEOSS) in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) Methods: Draft SoMES and MEOSS were co-produced from relevant literature and lived experience. An online survey completed by adults with ME/CFS and was repeated two weeks later to assess reliability. The SF-36 (physical function) assessed criterion-related validity (Spearmann correlations) and discriminant validity (Kruskal-Wallis tests). Weighted kappa co-efficients assessed test-retest reliability and measurement error calculated minimal detectable difference (MDD). Results: 995 adults with ME/CFS participated and 579 completed the retest survey. Construct validity was confirmed from feedback. Criterion related validity was moderate-good (SoMES r = 0.663, MEOSS r=0.472, both p<0.001). Discriminant validity was demonstrated by significant differences in SF36-PF scores in different levels of SoMES and MEOSS (p=0.003 - 0.0001). SoMES test-retest reliability was moderate (k =0.53, P<0.001) with a MDD of 1.6, and excellent for the MEOSS (k = 0.76 p<.001) and the MDD was 1.4 Conclusions: The Severity of ME Scale (SoMES) and the ME Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS) are valid, reliable, sensitive assessments of ME/CFS severity and occupational status respectively.

after.authors: Moreno-Armengol, A.; Blanco-Hinojo, L.; Casamitjana, L.; Gimenez-Palop, O.; Cobo, J.; Pujol, J.; Martinez-Vilavella, G.; Deus, J.; Esteba-Castillo, S.; Pareja, R.; Caixas, A.; Pena-Gomez, C.
after.abstract: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

after.authors: Kiwull, L.; Schmeder, V.; Zenker, M.; Mengual Hinojosa, M.; Kluger, G.; Eschermann, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Paracelsus Medical University, EURAS Project, Salzburg, Austria
after.abstract: Background SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SYNGAP1-DEE) is generally considered a haploinsufficiency disorder, yet language development varies considerably between affected individuals. With targeted therapies, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), approaching clinical evaluation, understanding genotype-specific differences is increasingly important. We investigated whether expressive language and functional communication are associated with SynGAP protein domains and variant class. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional caregiver-reported data linked to genetic reports from the international PATRE SYNGAP1 registry. Of 440 participants, 334 had variants that could be assigned to a protein domain and classified as missense (n=79) or truncating/splicing (n=255). Variants were mapped to seven predefined SynGAP protein regions. The primary outcome was a five-level current expressive language score. Secondary outcomes included acquisition of two-word phrases and CFCS-derived functional communication. Each domain was compared with all other regions within the same variant class using nonparametric tests and age-adjusted ordinal or logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results Missense variants in the C2 domain (aa248-392; n=28) were associated with markedly poorer expressive language (median score 1 vs. 2; age-adjusted OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06-0.46; q=0.0025). Only 7.1% had acquired two-word phrases compared with 52.0% of individuals with missense variants outside C2 (OR 0.07; q=0.0023). Functional communication was also significantly impaired (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09-0.56; q=0.0052). Conversely, truncating/splicing variants in the PH domain (aa103-247; n=50) were associated with better expressive language (median 3 vs. 2; OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.99-6.24; q<0.001) and more frequent acquisition of two-word phrases (62.0% vs. 31.5%). No corresponding language association was observed for C2 truncating/splicing variants or for variants in the RasGAP domain. Conclusions Language outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE are associated with both variant class and protein location. The marked impairment associated with C2 missense variants contrasts with the relatively preserved language abilities observed in PH truncating/splicing variants, suggesting that SYNGAP1-related disease cannot be fully explained by a uniform haploinsufficiency model alone. These findings support considering protein domain and variant class in future ASO trials, particularly for patient stratification, endpoint selection, and interpretation of treatment outcomes.

after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Opioids prescribed for acute pain frequently remain unused, creating opportunities for unintended use, accidental ingestion, or diversion. Little is known about counseling patients receive from prescribers or pharmacists on storage and disposal of opioids. OBJECTIVE: To characterize clinician counseling on opioid disposal and patient-reported storage, use, and disposal practices among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain. DESIGN: Multicenter prospective cohort study with participant recruitment between September 2020 and March 2023. PARTICIPANTS: Opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain in emergency departments, primary care or urgent care clinics, inpatient settings, and dental practices. MAIN MEASURES: Patient-reported receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods; opioid storage practices; use and disposition of prescribed opioids; disposal methods; and reasons for keeping or disposing of leftover opioids. KEY RESULTS: Among 1708 participants, the median age was 38 years (IQR, 28-52); most were recruited from emergency departments (n=915; 53.6%) and primary care or urgent care clinics (n=307; 18.0%). Among 1233 participants who answered the question on counseling about the importance of opioid disposal, 811 (65.8%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 1220 participants who answered the question on counseling about appropriate disposal methods, 832 (68.2%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 812 participants who answered the question about storing opioids in a locked location, 610 (75.1%) reported never doing so. Among 929 participants providing information on opioid leftovers and disposition, 618 (66.5%) did not use all prescribed opioids. Among these 618 participants, 258 (42.8%) kept leftover opioids and 345 (57.2%) disposed of them. Among 256 participants who reported reasons for keeping leftover opioids, 159 (62.1%) wanted medication available for the same condition, 70 (27.3%) wanted medication available for a different condition, and 36 (14.1%) did not know how to properly dispose of the medication. CONCLUSIONS: Among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, counseling about opioid disposal was uncommon, secure storage was infrequent, and leftover opioids were frequent, with many patients keeping leftover opioids for possible future use. These findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling on opioid storage and disposal and encourage safe disposal of unused opioids after acute pain treatment.

after.title: Preprint: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
after.authors: Li, S.; Xing, X.; Te, B.; Han, H.; Ji, H.; Yu, Y.; Siegel, L.; Lin, L.
after.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation.

after.authors: Chronister, B. N. C.; Parrish, E.; PARAJULI, R. P.; Lopez-Paredes, D.; Checkoway, H.; Suarez-Torres, J.; Quynh, A.; Martinez, D.; Bradman, A.; Suarez-Lopez, J. R.; Moore, R. C.
after.abstract: Objective: Emerging evidence suggests that exposure to organophosphate, neonicotinoid, and other pesticides may transiently impair cognition; however, traditional "snapshot" laboratory-based cognitive assessments fail to capture fluctuations in cognitive performance. This study used ecological momentary cognitive testing (EMCT) to evaluate whether real-world cognitive performance differs between peak and low floricultural pesticide spray seasons, thereby evaluating the potential cyclical effects of agricultural production and related pesticide exposures. Material and Methods: From 2022 to 2024, 15,063 EMCT assessments were completed by 494 participants (ages 17 to 25; 50% female) enrolled in the ESPINA cohort study in Ecuador. Participants completed nine 10-day burst assessments every 2 to 3 months during high and low pesticide spray seasons. EMCTs (NeuroUx) assessed processing speed, executive function, and visual working memory. Mixed-effects models examined associations of peak versus off-peak pesticide spray seasons, floricultural work or occupation (vs not) with EMCT performance, adjusting for socio-economic and other variables, and including participant- and burst-level random intercepts. Results: Peak pesticide spray season, compared to off-peak, was associated with higher T-scores on processing speed tests, including Matching Pair (B= 0.62) and Odd One Out (B= 0.88), but showed no significant association with other tests or the overall cognitive composite. Conversely, direct floricultural employment was significantly associated with lower cognitive performance overall (B= -0.59), with the largest differences observed in Memory Matrix (B= -0.78) and Matching Pair (B= -0.70). Conclusion: Peak pesticide spray seasons were associated with modestly higher processing speed scores, consistent with prior findings in this population suggestive of enhanced cognitive performance associated with neonicotinoid and sulfoximine exposures. In contrast, floricultural employment was associated with significantly lower memory and overall cognitive performance. These results suggest that occupational and seasonal pesticide exposure may have distinct associations with cognitive functioning, highlighting the importance of repeated cognitive testing for characterizing potentially transient effects.

after.authors: pious, I. S.; Beyeza-Kashesya, J.; Namagembe, I.; Twesigemukama, S.; Godfrey James, A.; Saad Sessimba, K.; Balikudembe, K.; Andrew, B.; Mary, M.; Mwanje, D.; Musanje, K.; Sekikubo, M.
after.abstract: Abstract Background: The Copper-T intrauterine device (Cu-T IUD) is a highly effective, non-hormonal, long-acting reversible contraceptive that can protect against pregnancy for up to 12 years, with a failure rate under 1%. Despite its clinical efficacy, early discontinuation remains a substantial challenge in Uganda, where discontinuation is approximated at 29% within the first year of use. Understanding the experiences of women using the Cu-T IUD is important to predict factors associated with discontinuation and to inform practice. Methods: Between September and November 2025, we conducted twenty in-depth interviews with women of reproductive age (15-49 years) who had used a Cu-T IUD for at least two years, recruited from the family planning clinic of Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Kampala, Uganda. Data were analysed thematically, guided by the Social-Ecological Model and Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping. Results: Long-term Cu-T IUD users reported both positive and negative experiences shaped by individual, interpersonal, and community factors. Two themes were identified at the individual-level domain: experiences during insertion and post-insertion experiences. Negative experiences, particularly heavy menstrual bleeding, anxiety, and abdominal pain, were common and distressing. Participants employed coping strategies, including taking painkillers, using home remedies, and resting, to manage these challenges with Cu-T IUD use. Conclusions: Negative experiences of Cu-T IUD are common among long-term users; women's coping strategies such as taking painkillers lead to continued use. Client-centred pre-insertion counselling addressing both anticipated side effects and common misconceptions, alongside accessible follow-up services, may facilitate long-term Cu-T IUD use. Keywords: copper-T IUD; lived experiences; coping mechanisms; long-term use; Uganda

after.title: Preprint: Efficacy and Clinical Predictors of Topical NSAIDs as Bridging Therapy for Diabetic Macular Edema: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
after.authors: Roikhan, M. A.; Rahmah, F. S.
after.abstract: Introduction & Objectives: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is a primary cause of vision loss. While anti-VEGF injections are the gold standard, prolonged referral delays in primary care settings often lead to irreversible photoreceptor damage. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of topical Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) as a temporary bridging therapy and to develop a new clinical scoring system to guide primary care physicians in early intervention. Methods: A systematic review was conducted to identify clinical predictors of responses to topical NSAIDs in DME patients, followed by a meta-analysis to calculate pooled Odds Ratios (OR) for each predictor. These values underwent natural log transformation (beta = ln(OR)) to derive a point-based clinical scoring system. Result: Twelve studies were analyzed. Predictor variables and assigned points derived from pooled ORs included: glycemic control (HbA1c < 8.0%; OR 2.41, 9 points), symptom duration (< 6 months; OR 2.11, 7 points), baseline visual acuity (> 6/12; OR 1.96, 7 points), and retinopathy stage (mild-to-moderate NPDR; OR 1.77, 5 points). The proposed 28-point scoring system categorizes patients into three tiers: High Probability (21-28 points) for immediate NSAID initiation; Moderate Probability (12-20 points) for combined systemic optimization; and Low Probability (0-11 points) for prioritized emergency referral. Evidence confirms that potent topical NSAIDs effectively stabilize macular thickness and prevent exudative progression during the referral window. Conclusion: This study concludes that the OR-derived scoring system effectively empowers primary care physicians to manage DME during referral windows. Topical NSAIDs serve as a safe, low-risk bridging strategy to mitigate permanent vision loss and reduce the burden of blindness in resource-limited settings.

after.authors: Truyen, T. T. T. T.; Chugh, H.; Nguyen, D.; Nakamura, K.; Uy-Evanado, A.; Benjamin, E. J.; Reinier, K.; Chugh, S. S.
after.abstract: Background: Sex differences in sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) incidence and outcomes are well established, but risk stratification underperforms in women. It is important to delineate sex-specific patterns in SCA across clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic domains. Methods: We studied out-of-hospital SCA cases from the Oregon Sudden Unexpected Death Study (ORSUDS; Portland, 2002-2020; discovery) and Prediction of Sudden Death in Multi-Ethnic Communities (PRESTO; Ventura County, 2015-2024; external replication). Sex differences in 38 comorbidities, 19 ECG and 12 echocardiographic measures were estimated using multivariable-adjusted logistic regression. Female sex was the modeled dependent measure (male as reference). ORSUDS estimates were compared with those in the Framingham Heart Study (FHS), a community-based reference cohort, using FDR-adjusted Cochran Q tests. Results: Among 5130 ORSUDS cases, 1715 (33.4%) were women (median age, 70.4 years [IQR, 58.7-81.8]) and 3415 (66.6%) were men (65.6 [55.0-76.8]). Compared with men, women had higher BMI (per 5 kg/m2, 1.11 [1.08-1.15]) and higher odds of thyroid disease (2.56 [2.17-3.13]), asthma (2.33 [1.92-2.86]), mood disorder (2.17 [1.85-2.50]), dementia (1.27 [1.02-1.56]), and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH, 3.13 [2.44-4.00]). Women also had lower odds of coronary artery disease (0.61 [0.52-0.71]), atrial fibrillation (0.67 [0.56-0.79]), prolonged QTc (0.45 [0.35-0.57]), prolonged PR (0.53 [0.41-0.68]), premature contractions (0.77 [0.60-0.98]), sleep apnea (0.53 [0.43-0.65]), and reduced LVEF (0.40 [0.29-0.54]). Most findings were replicated in PRESTO (n=2719). In contrast, several of these differences were reversed in the community (FHS, n=3539;FDR-significant): prolonged QTc was more common in women, whereas LVH, dementia, heart failure, and higher BMI were more common in men. Conclusions: Sex differences among SCA cases were mostly reproducible in SCA cohorts, and distinct from sex-related patterns in the community. These results have implications for development of sex-specific SCA risk assessment and prevention strategies.

after.title: Preprint: Improvements in patient-reported outcomes after neuromuscular electrical stimulation therapy for snoring and mild sleep apnea
after.authors: Crawford, M. R.; Jones, A. L.; Parthasarathy, S.; Osborne, C.; Walia, H.; Ojile, J.; Malhotra, A.
after.abstract: Objectives: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) offers alternative options to patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) unable to tolerate first line treatment. Randomized controlled trial data suggest efficacy of NMES treatment in improving OSA outcomes, snoring and sleepiness; however, no study to our knowledge has examined the effects on a range of daytime patient reported outcomes in a large real-world sample. Methods: This report presents clinical data from 472 patients completing NMES treatment. Bayesian linear mixed models were used to analyze pre-to-post treatment changes in mood (PHQ8), sleep disturbance (PROMIS-SD-4a), sleep related impairment (PROMIS-SRI-4a), and functioning (FOSQ), whilst controlling for key covariates. Posterior probabilities were calculated to estimate the probability of a change in symptoms (P(effect > 0)) and probability of exceeding a minimal clinically important difference (P(effect > MCID)). Results: The posterior probabilities of an improvement in scores in sleep disturbance (mean change -6.1, 94% HDI: -3.8 to -8.5) and sleep-related impairment (mean change -10.0, 94% HDI: -5.4 to -14), depression (mean change -3.5, 94% HDI: -1.7 to -5.2), at posttreatment were greatest and varied between 99.8 to 100%. Probability of change in functioning was low (60.9% chance of improvement). These effects remained when controlling for age, gender, treatment adherence, mean intensity and variance in intensity. Probabilities for MCI change for mood, sleep disturbance and sleep-related impairment were high (86-91%). Conclusions: The results from this report highlight the potential impact NMES therapy has on patient reported outcomes. These findings are in support of prior randomized placebo-controlled data and several observational cohort studies for NMES as treatment for mild OSA.

after.authors: Ha, L. T.; Ver Donck, F.; Bassez, I.; Oeste, C. L.; Vulsteke, C.; Delombaerde, D.; Hens, D.; Prenen, H.; Croes, L.; De Meulenaere, A.; Debruyne, P. R.; Verhaert, M.; Aspeslagh, S.; Brusselaers, N.; Verbiest, A.
after.abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, yet evidence on their utilization, treatment trajectories, and effectiveness in routine clinical practice remains limited. We characterized real-world ICI use and outcomes across cancer types using the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort and explored differences between real-world and pivotal trial outcomes. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals. Structured and unstructured electronic health record data were harmonized using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) and natural language processing. We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival. OS was descriptively compared with pivotal trials, and prognostic factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression. An interactive public dashboard was developed to enable exploration of cohort characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes. Results: Among 3,231 ICI-treated patients, 2,514 (77.8%) had metastatic disease. Among metastatic patients, 568 (22.6%) discontinued ICI without subsequent systemic therapy. Median post-discontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2), with 49.1% alive at 24 months. ToT and TTNT were generally shorter than OS, particularly in melanoma (median OS 78 months; ToT 7 months; TTNT 26 months). Real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials. ECOG >=2 was associated with poorer OS than ECOG 0-1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60). In NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated trial outcomes, whereas survival with ECOG >=2 was substantially poorer. Conclusions: Real-world ICI treatment trajectories extend beyond active treatment, with some patients experiencing prolonged survival after discontinuation. Differences between real-world and trial outcomes highlight the importance of patient characteristics, particularly performance status, when interpreting trial evidence in routine care. FAIR-ICI provides a scalable framework for evaluating real-world immunotherapy effectiveness, treatment trajectories, and future investigations of treatment-related toxicity.

after.authors: Ferreira Jorgensen, C.; Chillon, T. S.; Scavenius, C.; Sacks, D. B.; Raghuraman, B.; Bekker-Nielsen, D.; Bache, N.; Vorm, O.; Rode, L.; Ekelund, C.; Damm, P.; Hojlund, K.; Jensen, D. M.; Clausen, T. D.; McIntyre, H. D.; Overgaard, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Clinical Biochemistry, Odense University Hospital, Odense, Denmark
after.abstract: Aims/hypothesis Glycated albumin (GA) has been shown to be a moderate predictor of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), while evidence supporting its role in predicting adverse pregnancy outcomes remains limited. Here, we aimed to perform a comparative study of GA and haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) for predicting GDM and large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants in a prospective cohort. Methods We developed a rapid liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry method for measuring site-specific albumin glycation. GA was quantified at two glycation sites, GA (KQT) and GA (KLV), as well as their sum, GA-total. GA was measured in stored serum samples collected at 11-14 and 23-31 gestational weeks from 465 participants in the single-centre observational cohort. HbA1c was measured routinely at each visit. Linear mixed-effects models were used to compare GA between participants with and without GDM (n=100) or LGA (n=57). Logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) for GDM and LGA according to GA and HbA1c. Results GA was lower in women who developed GDM during early pregnancy compared to non-GDM controls (GA-total; p=0.004), while in mid-late pregnancy, only GA (KQT) was lower in women with GDM (p=0.036). In contrast, HbA1c was higher in women with GDM at both timepoints compared to non-GDM controls (p<0.001) and higher HbA1c was associated with increased odds of GDM (OR=2.20, p<0.001; OR=2.30, p<0.001, respectively). GA was higher in the LGA group, in both early (GA-total; p=0.032) and mid-late pregnancy (GA-total; p=0.030) and associated with increased odds of LGA (GA-total; OR=1.59, p=0.009; GA-total; OR=1.46, p=0.019, respectively). HbA1c was not associated with LGA at either timepoint. Conclusions/interpretation Higher GA in early and mid-late pregnancy were associated with an increased risk of LGA, whereas no significant association was observed for HbA1c. GA may therefore provide risk assessment beyond HbA1c for identifying pregnancies at risk of fetal overgrowth.

after.title: Preprint: Cerebral white matter integrity in Type-2 Diabetes Mellitus and integrated role of Interleukin-6: Findings in multiethnic middle-aged and older US-adults
after.authors: Hallab, A.; The Health and Aging Brain Study (HABS-HD) Study Team,
after.abstract: Introduction: Peripheral neural injuries, known as polyneuropathy, are largely described in patients with Type-2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM). However, less is known about the T2DM-associated cerebral White Matter (WM) integrity. Previous studies highlighted mediating effects of inflammation in the T2DM-brain association. It is, however, still unclear whether Interleukin-6 (IL-6) mediates specifically T2DM-cerebral WM integrity. Methods: The multiethnic 50 years and older study population is a subset of the Health and Aging Brain Study: Health Disparities (HABS-HD) study. Diffusion-weighted scans were analyzed, and diffusion parameters were averaged in major WM tracts. Effect sizes (Cohen s d) were calculated after adjusting for relevant confounders. Mediation analysis was performed using 1000-fold non-parametric bootstrapping of 95% confidence intervals (CI). The results were adjusted for multiple testing using the False Discovery Rate method (FDR). Results: Several WM tracts showed significant impairment in T2DM participants after adjusting for confounders and multiple testing (posterior thalamic radiation (adj. Cohen s d=0.14[0.03-024]), anterior corona radiata (adj. Cohen s d=0.15[0.04-0.26]), cingulum (adj. Cohen s d=0.14[0.03-0.25]), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (adj. Cohen s d=0.16[0.06-0.27]), genu of the corpus callosum (adj. Cohen s d=0.13[0.03-0.24]), and body of the corpus callosum (adj. Cohen s d=0.28[0.17-0.38])). Within two years, the effect sizes showed an increasing trend. Even in cognitively unimpaired participants, T2DM was associated with locally reduced WM integrity. IL-6 statistically mediated up to 15% of these major associations. Conclusions: The study demonstrated T2DM-associated impairment of intracerebral WM integrity. In T2DM, microstructural WM changes might start before clinically objectified cognitive impairment. The role of systemic inflammation needs to be assessed in causal frameworks.

after.title: Preprint: Target Trial Emulation of Metformin for Dementia Prevention in All of Us: Robustness to Cohort and Confounder Definitions
after.authors: Charpignon, M.-L.; Shnitzer, T.; Iraqui, A.; Pace, D. F.; Maddah, M.; Uhler, C.
after.abstract: Metformin use has been associated with a lower risk of incident dementia than other antidiabetics. We perform target trial emulation and causal competing risk analysis in the NIH All of Us (AoU) Research Program database, contrasting the effects of metformin and sulfonylurea initiation on dementia onset and death without dementia. AoU's social and behavioral health data allowed us to test robustness to excluding such confounders, and we further adjusted for calendar year effects and prior antidiabetic exposure, using both semiparametric Cox proportional hazards (PH) models and nonparametric models. Under stabilized inverse propensity score of treatment weighting, metformin was associated with a substantially lower risk of death (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.61, 95% CI: [0.49, 0.75]) and a lower incidence of dementia (HR: 0.90, 95% CI: [0.82, 1.02]). Estimated HRs were closely aligned with estimates obtained in the UK primary care and US Mass General Brigham health systems. This finding was robust to the inclusion of participants without a type 2 diabetes diagnosis at baseline and to the consideration of different covariate sets in the propensity score model, supporting metformin as a promising candidate for dementia prevention and motivating prospective validation.

after.title: Preprint: Association between trajectories of breastfeeding duration and infant health: Prospective cohort study
after.authors: Dessy, T.; Dennis, C.-L.
after.abstract: Background: Breastfeeding is a modifiable pathway contributing to infant health. Objectives: To estimate trajectories of breastfeeding and the association between trajectories of breastfeeding and infant health. Methods: We conducted a prospective longitudinal cohort study (2014-2020, Canada) with 3217 cohabitating English-literate mother-father-infant triads with internet or telephone access. Women with major psychiatric conditions or suicidality were excluded. Data were collected online at baseline (<3 weeks postpartum), 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months. Breastfeeding was measured at 0-12 months. Baseline measures included attention-deficit disorder with/without hyperactivity (ADHD, Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale) and childhood adversity (Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire). We measured infant health at 12-24 months using the Brief Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (challenging behaviors) and self-reported number of emergent visits (>90th percentile). We estimated trajectories of breastfeeding using latent class growth analysis. Associations were estimated using adjusted linear mixed models. Results: Most included mothers (n=2548) were of Canadian birth (2078/2548, 82%) and graduated from university (1920/2548, 75%); few reported unemployment (222/2548, 9%) or prenatal depression (240/2548, 9%). We identified two trajectories of breastfeeding: Constant Breastfeeding (1522/2548, 60%) and Decreasing Breastfeeding (1026/2548, 40%). No statistically significant differences were observed between classes for either the risk of challenging behaviors (RR -0.006 95% CI -0.028 to 0.016) or the risk of emergent visits (RR -0.015 95% CI -0.053 to 0.023). Conclusions: In this study, discontinued breastfeeding was not associated with infant health. Future studies should focus on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding, a modifiable therapeutic infant feeding target.

after.title: Preprint: Maternal ADHD and exclusive breastfeeding: A prospective community-based cohort study
after.authors: Dessy, T.; Dennis, C.-L.
after.abstract: Importance: Maternal attention-deficit disorder with or without hyperactivity (ADHD) is an established risk factor for adverse perinatal outcomes that remains understudied to breastfeeding. Objective: To estimate the effect of maternal ADHD on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding. Design: A prospective longitudinal community-based cohort study. Setting: Canada, 2014-2020. Participants: We included 3217 English-literate mother-father dyads with internet or telephone access, comprising women with singleton birth within 3 weeks postpartum (study baseline) and were cohabiting with the biological father. Women with major psychiatric conditions or suicidality were excluded. All participants provided informed consent at recruitment. Data were collected online through self-report questionnaires. Exposure: Maternal ADHD was measured at baseline using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (sum of scores [≥]14). Main Outcomes and Measures: We defined 6-month exclusive breastfeeding based on maternal reported infant feeding, assessed at 3 and 6 months. Maternal childhood adversity (Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire, ACE-IQ; sum score) was included as a confounder. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) was estimated using linear probability models. We calculated 95% percentile bootstrap CI. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with 10 iterations. Results: Complete-case analyses included 2071/3217 mother-father dyads, most of which were Canadian-born (79%). Childhood adversity, mental health conditions, and substance use were higher among mothers who screened positive for ADHD (4%) than among those who did not: the median number of ACE was 5 IQR 4-6; 38% self-reported prenatal depression, 13% smoked cigarettes and 19% drank alcohol during pregnancy; 11% of infants used the neonatal intensive care unit. Notably, though 90% of mothers with ADHD intended to breastfeed exclusively only 28% breastfed exclusively for 6 months. Among families with maternal ADHD, the effect of maternal ADHD on 6-month exclusive breastfeeding was ATT -0.105, 95% CI -0.209 to -0.003 in the model adjusted for maternal ACE and paternal ADHD. With multiple imputation: ATT -0.109, 95% CI -0.213 to -0.004. Conclusions and Relevance: Mothers with ADHD intend to breastfeed their infants exclusively, but additional challenges shorten the duration of exclusive breastfeeding, indicating a need for interventions tailored to neurodevelopmental differences.

after.title: Preprint: Polydrug use and recreational motives are associated with lower posttraumatic symptoms in survivors of a mass trauma event
after.authors: Magal, N.; Netzer, O.; Epstein, D. H.; Shaham, Y.; Repantis, D.; Lev-Ran, S.; Harduf, A.; Admon, R.; Salomon, R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: School of Psychological Sciences, University of Haifa, Haifa, Israel; Integrated Brain and Behavior Research Center (IBBRC), University of Haifa, Haifa, Israel;
after.abstract: Objective: Drug use after trauma is common, but polydrug use patterns, motives, and associations with subsequent symptoms are poorly understood. We examined these associations among mass-casualty terror attack survivors, 72% of whom used drugs immediately before trauma exposure. Methods: Survivors of the October 7, 2023 Nova Festival attack reported use of six drug types (alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, stimulants, MDMA, psychedelics) and motives (avoidance, emotional regulation, self-medication, sleep, recreation) longitudinally at three timepoints (TP): 1-6 months (N=772), 8-12 months (N=453), and 17-24 months (N=302) post-attack. Separate latent class analyses of TP2 data characterized drug use, motives, and their combination. Linear regression and mixed-effects models examined associations between class membership and PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) scores, adjusting for age, sex, time since trauma, and TP1 PCL-5 scores. Results: At TP2, 70% reported polydrug use, 17% used one drug, and 13% reported no use. The high drug-load class (mean 4.6 drug types) had lower PCL-5 scores than the low drug-load class (mean 1.5 drug types); this difference was evident among participants using [≥]4 drug types and persisted through TP3. The self-medication-motive class had higher PCL-5 scores than the recreational-motive class. In joint analyses, recreational-motive users at both low and high drug loads had lower PCL-5 scores than participants reporting self-medication motives and primarily cannabis use. Conclusions: Polydrug use was common among the mass-trauma survivors in our study. Self-medication motives were associated with higher PTSD symptom severity than recreational motives. Unexpectedly, higher polydrug use was associated with lower PTSD symptom scores.

after.authors: Iacoban, C. G.; Klüner, C.; Bösenberg, H.; Alykova, O.; Gerdes, M.; Reuter, S.; Mathys, C.; Sundermann, B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Radiology and Neuroradiology, Evangelisches Krankenhaus Oldenburg, Steinweg 13-17, 26122 Oldenburg, Niedersachsen, Germany
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: 3D-FLAIR is central to MR-based diagnosis and monitoring of MS, but long acquisition times remain a limitation. OBJECTIVES: This single-center prospective non-inferiority study evaluated whether compressed sensing (CS) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR at 1.5T provides lesion detection comparable to optimized Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR. Optimized CS- and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR sequences were incorporated into MRI examinations in patients with known or suspected MS. The primary endpoint was manual lesion count by two blinded readers using a 10% non-inferiority margin. Secondary endpoints included image quality, SNR, CNR, and automated lesion count and volumetry. RESULTS: Sixty-eight patients were included (mean age, 40.1+/-13.3 years; 61.8% women). CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR reduced acquisition time by 31.8% compared with GRAPPA (4:00 vs 5:52 minutes). Non-inferiority for manual lesion count was demonstrated for both readers (reader A, p < .0001; reader B, p = .005). Interrater agreement was excellent for CS (ICC = 0.921; 95% CI, 0.837-0.957) and very good for GRAPPA (ICC = 0.851; 95% CI, 0.769-0.906). Subjective image quality was high for both techniques. GRAPPA showed higher objective signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR), whereas automated lesion counts and volumes were higher for CS. CONCLUSION: CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR provided non-inferior lesion detection with substantial scan-time reduction.

Interrater agreement was excellent for CS (ICC = 0.921; 95% CI, 0.837-0.957) and very good for GRAPPA (ICC = 0.851; 95% CI, 0.769-0.906). Subjective image quality was high for both techniques. GRAPPA showed higher objective signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR), whereas automated lesion counts and volumes were higher for CS. CONCLUSION: CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR provided non-inferior lesion detection with substantial scan-time reduction.

after.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES 3D-TOF-MRA is a standard non-invasive method for detecting and monitoring intracranial aneurysms, but long scan times remain a limitation. Compressed sensing (CS) acceleration for intracranial aneurysm evaluation has mainly been studied at 3T. This prospective single-center non-inferiority study compared CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T with GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF-MRA for evaluating untreated intracranial aneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODS Sample size was determined via a preliminary retrospective study. 25 patients with 32 untreated aneurysms underwent both CS- (factor 7, 3:04 min) and GRAPPA-accelerated (factor 2, 5:00 min) 3D-TOF, yielding a 38.7% scan-time reduction. Two blinded neuroradiologists assessed overall image quality (primary endpoint) and artifacts, subjective CNR, aneurysm delineation and diameters (secondary endpoints). Non-inferiority was tested via one-sided t-test (prespecified 10% margin); interrater agreement used ICC. RESULTS CS demonstrated non-inferiority to GRAPPA for overall image quality in both readers (p <= .023), though interrater agreement was low (ICC 0.241-0.262), reflecting subjective variability. Secondary exploratory analyses showed heterogeneous preferences. ROI-based CNR was lower for CS (median 169.6; IQR, 91.0-226. vs. 278.2; 181.0-366.2). Aneurysm diameter measurements showed excellent interrater agreement for both techniques (CS ICC, 0.899-0.980; GRAPPA ICC, 0.877-0.973; all p < .001). CONCLUSION CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T met non-inferiority criteria vs. GRAPPA-TOF for overall image quality, reducing scan time by 38.7% while preserving aneurysm measurement reliability. However, reduced CNR and reader-preference variability important trade-offs.

after.authors: Weustink, A. C.; Keijzer, A. R.; Budde, R. P. J.; Versmissen, J.; Galema, T. W.; Veen, K. M.; Takkenberg, J. J. M.; Arabkhani, B.; Coenen, A.
after.abstract: Objectives: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non inflammatory, non atherosclerotic arterial disease characterized by multifocal arterial beading that predominantly affects women. Although FMD commonly involves the renal and carotid arteries, its relationship with acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) remains poorly understood. We investigated the proportion of patients with FMD among patients with ATAAD, focusing on sex based differences. Materials and Methods: Patients aged below 70 years with ATAAD and ECG triggered aortic CT angiography (CTA) were consecutively included in this retrospective single-center study. FMD was defined as multifocal arterial beading (string-of-beads appearance) in at least one vascular territory, according to international consensus criteria. The highest-quality CTA examination was evaluated by an experienced cardiovascular radiologist. All suspected FMD cases were independently reviewed by a second experienced cardiovascular radiologist, with the final diagnosis established by consensus. Proportions were reported with 95% confidence intervals and compared between sexes . Results: Of 214 patients screened, 200 were included (138 men and 62 women). FMD was confirmed in 18/200 patients (9%; 95% CI, 6 till 14%), none of whom had a prior FMD diagnosis. FMD was more frequent in women (12/62, 19%; 95% CI, 11 till 31%) than men (6/138, 4%; 95% CI, 2 till 9%; P<0.001). FMD predominantly involved the renal arteries. Additional carotid CTA was available in 49/200 patients (25%) and in 7/18 patients with FMD (39%); three of these seven patients had carotid FMD. Conclusion: FMD was observed in a substantial proportion of patients presenting with ATAAD, particularly women. These findings suggest that FMD is an underrecognized vascular phenotype in patients with ATAAD.

after.authors: Copoeru, A. D.; Mocan, M.; Farcas, A.; Vlaicu, S.; Chira, R. I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: "Iuliu Hatieganu" University of Medicine and Pharmacy
after.abstract: Interstitial lung diseases (ILD) associated with systemic autoimmune disease can have a strong negative impact on patient outcomes. The diagnostic gold standard is high-resolution computer tomography (HRCT). Numerous studies have proven lung ultrasound's (LUS) utility in ILD, as well as other lung pathologies. Recently, there has been more focus on ILD in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a previously overlooked complication, and screening methods. The purpose of this systematic review was to summarize the recent knowledge regarding LUS compared to HRCT in screening ILD in RA patients. We reviewed relevant literature from the last 10 years and selected 10 articles. Results show that LUS is effective compared to HRCT as a screening tool. Several diagnostic and severity scores have been elaborated and tested. Further focus should be on LUS in long-term follow-up and standardization of protocols.

after.abstract: Background: Cognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep- could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. Methods: PD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. Discussion: The PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS' disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases.

after.abstract: Background and Objectives: Motor dysfunction is a major contributor to disability in pediatric-onset monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet systematic quantifications of motor phenotypes across development using validated clinical scales remain underdeveloped. Existing studies have classified motor phenotypes rather than quantified domain-specific severity, limiting their use as outcome measures in clinical trials. Here, we systematically quantify motor dysfunction using established clinical rating scales to explore their utility as motor endpoints. Methods: In this cross-sectional observational study, 102 individuals with NDDs (0.5-38 years) secondary to pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in five genes (SCN2A, KCNQ2, CSNK2A1, CACNA1A, SCN8A) and 31 unaffected sibling controls underwent standardized motor assessments using the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia, Burke-Fahn-Marsden Dystonia Scale, and the Modified Ashworth Scale. Regional and functional categorization of parameters enabled differentiated interpretation. Gene-specific patterns were evaluated using z-score standardization across the pooled affected cohort, with gene-level averaging and nonparametric bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals. Results: Dysfunction was present in individuals with NDDs across speech (90%), coordination (87%), dystonia (83.3%), gross motor (82.4%) and spasticity (42.2%), with minimal impairment in controls (0-12.9%). We observed substantial heterogeneity across motor domains and subdomains; ataxic dysarthria had the highest score distribution (median 0.83 [IQR, 0.17-1.0]), whereas spasticity showed near-floor scores. Individuals with SCN2A variants demonstrated higher mean z-scores across multiple subdomains than other genes, with more consistent deviations observed in coordination and speech domains (Coordination: mean z = 0.29, 95% CI 0.03-0.54; Speech: mean z = 0.3, 95% CI 0.03-0.57), whereas domain-specific or less pronounced patterns were observed in other genes. The ataxia and dystonia scales demonstrated low floor and ceiling effects. Discussion: Using three clinical scales across a broad developmental and functional range, our study moves motor phenotyping in monogenic NDDs from categorical description toward quantitative, domain-resolved severity assessment. Exploratory analysis indicates marked heterogeneity in severity profiles across genes, most notably in SCN2A, suggesting potential selective motor vulnerability. These findings provide evidence for the feasibility of motor phenotyping and provide preliminary, cross-sectional benchmark severity distributions. Subsequent longitudinal validation and validation in larger, longitudinal, and variant-stratified cohorts will enable natural history studies and future therapeutic trials alongside seizure outcomes.

after.abstract: Purpose: This study, conducted by the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel (ClinGen SCID-VCEP), aimed to adapt the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) framework for germline variant interpretation in RMRP. Unlike the protein-coding genes for which the framework was primarily developed, RMRP encodes a non-protein-coding RNA. Biallelic pathogenic variants in RMRP cause cartilage-hair hypoplasia, which can include severe combined immunodeficiency disease and other immune abnormalities. Methods: An RMRP-focused SCID-VCEP subgroup reviewed all 28 ACMG/AMP evidence criteria using population databases, published clinical and experimental data, computational predictions, and expert consensus. Each criterion was retained, modified, or designated as not applicable based on RMRP biology and disease mechanisms. The resulting specifications were pilot tested using 27 variants selected from ClinVar and research laboratory data. Results: Fifteen ACMG/AMP criteria were determined to be applicable to RMRP, while 13 were considered not applicable. Several criteria were modified to evaluate nucleotide-level effects on transcriptional regulation, critical promoter regions, and RNA secondary structure. The specifications also incorporated RMRP-specific recommendations for population frequency, functional evidence, variant phase, segregation, and phenotype. Application of the specifications classified 6 variants as pathogenic, 10 as likely pathogenic, 7 as variants of uncertain significance, and 4 as benign. Previously pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants remained within the pathogenic spectrum, and all previously benign variants remained benign. Variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations were resolved as either likely pathogenic or uncertain. PM1, PM3, and PP4 were the primary criteria supporting pathogenic classifications. Conclusion: The SCID-VCEP specifications provide a standardized approach to the classification of germline RMRP variants in cartilage-hair hypoplasia and demonstrate how the ACMG/AMP framework can be adapted for a disease-associated non-protein-coding RNA gene. These specifications support the development of variant interpretation frameworks for other clinically relevant non-protein-coding genes.

G.; Ostermann, M.; Muscedere, J.; Marshall, J.; Deane, A.; Lauzier, F.; Arabi, Y. M.; Kuriyama, A.; Burns, K.; Yarnell, C. J.; Vazquez Grande, G.; Zytaruk, N.; Cook, D. after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Background A recent international randomized trial found that the proton pump inhibitor (PPI) pantoprazole significantly reduced the risk of clinically important upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding among invasively ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU), with no effect on mortality. Pantoprazole may be of particularly high utility among patients at high-risk of bleeding, such as those receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) prior to ICU admission. However, given the complex mechanisms by which renal insufficiency may increase bleeding risk, as well as the possible association between PPI use and adverse kidney outcomes, investigating whether kidney failure treated with RRT at baseline modifies the treatment effect of PPIs is clinically relevant. Methods We have planned a post hoc secondary analysis of the Re-evaluating the Inhibition of Stress Erosions (REVISE) Trial (NCT03374800). The primary objective if this study is to evaluate whether any RRT on study day 1 (e.g., maintenance RRT in the outpatient setting, or RRT initiated in the hospital [intermittent hemodialysis, continuous renal replacement therapy, sustained low efficiency dialysis, or peritoneal dialysis]) modifies the treatment effect of pantoprazole on clinically important upper GI bleeding and 90-day mortality. The secondary objective is to evaluate whether maintenance RRT (intermittent hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) in an outpatient setting before the index hospital admission modifies the effect of pantoprazole on clinically important upper GI bleeding and 90-day mortality. Secondary outcomes for both analyses are patient important upper GI bleeding, ICU and hospital mortality. We will perform Cox proportional-hazard analyses, including the RRT exposure of interest, randomized group, and their interaction for each outcome, reporting results as hazards ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and p-values for the interaction term. Conclusion Results of this study will inform critical care practice, particularly for the care of patients at risk of stress-related GI ulceration in the ICU who have received RRT.

after.title: Preprint: Oral rehydration salts and zinc for childhood diarrhoea in Bangladesh, 2019 and 2025: coverage, wealth inequality and reported source of care
after.authors: Hoque, S. M. A. U.; Hasan, M. K.; Rahman, M. A.; Islam, M. K.; Ahmed, T.; Haque, S. M. R.; Islam, M. R.; Baset, K. u.
after.abstract: Background: Diarrhoea remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children under five. WHO and UNICEF recommend oral rehydration salts (ORS) alongside 10 to 14 days of zinc supplementation. However, national progress in combined treatment coverage and its socioeconomic and care-related inequalities remains insufficiently understood in Bangladesh. We assessed combined coverage, wealth inequality and differences by reported source of care. Methods: We analysed children under five with caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the 2019 (n=1,589) and 2025 (n=1,634) Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS). We estimated combined coverage using design-based methods, wealth inequality using slope indices, and associations with source of care using pooled adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR). Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) estimates provided an external comparison. Results: Combined ORS and zinc coverage increased from 35.0% (95% CI 32.3 to 37.7) in 2019 to 42.9% (40.1 to 45.8) in 2025. In 2025, ORS and zinc coverage were 75.8% and 51.9%, respectively. The 2025 estimate agreed with DHS 2022, whereas MICS 2019 was below DHS 2017-18. Wealth inequality persisted in 2025 (slope index 13.0 percentage points, 3.4 to 22.6). Adjustment attenuated the pooled slope index from 11.8 to 6.5 points (-1.7 to 14.6). Coverage was lower with pharmacy-only than public care (aPR 0.59, 0.53 to 0.66) and with no care reported (0.14, 0.11 to 0.18). Children with no care reported accounted for 43.7% of children without combined treatment in 2025. Conclusions: Combined coverage increased, although the apparent progress may be overstated by the lower MICS 2019 estimate relative to DHS. Zinc remained the larger treatment gap, while one in four children received no ORS. Reported sources of care require cautious interpretation.

after.title: Preprint: The impact of warning labels versus traffic light labels on food choice and negative emotional responses: two randomised controlled trials among UK adult populations with and without an eating disorder
after.authors: Evans, R. K.; Latham, R.; Finlay, A.; Robinson, E.
after.abstract: Background In the UK, front-of-pack traffic light labels (TLL) are implemented voluntarily. The UK Government are considering alternative FOP approaches, such as nutrient warning labels (WL). However, the effects and potential harm of TLL versus WL in UK consumers are unclear. We compared the effects of WL, TLL, and no label on unhealthy food item selection and negative affect among UK adults with and without an eating disorder (ED). Methods We conducted two online randomised controlled trials. In Study 1, 924 UK adults without an ED diagnosis were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to a WL, TLL, or no labels condition and completed a food-choice task. In Study 2, 240 UK adults with an ED diagnosis completed a baseline no-label food choice task and were subsequently randomly assigned (1:1:1) to WL, TLL, or no labels for a follow-up food choice task. The primary outcome was the number of task-specific unhealthy food items selected. Negative affect before and after food choice tasks was measured as a secondary outcome. Findings In Study 1 (data collected 02/25 - 04/25), unhealthy food selection differed by condition (p = .013). Of five products selected, WL participants selected 0.20 fewer unhealthy items than TLL participants (8.0%; p = .038) and 0.28 fewer than controls (10.7%; p = .004). In Study 2 (data collected 11/25 - 02/26), unhealthy selection decreased by 0.39 items with WL (17.7%; p = .015), 0.13 with TLL (5.3%, p = .286), and 0.00 with no labels. The reduction was greater with WL than with no labels (p = .029). Label condition did not differentially affect task-related negative affect in either study (Study 1, p = .757; Study 2, p = .448). Interpretation WL tended to be associated with lower unhealthy food selection compared to TLL in UK adults. There was minimal evidence that WL or TLL caused negative emotional responses. Funding This research was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Oxford Health BRC. The views expressed are those of the author(s) and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care. Registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07339969

after.title: Preprint: Diagnostic Feature Associations in Atypical Parkinsonian Disorders: A Survey of Movement Disorders Specialists
after.authors: Zweber, C.; Iyer, V.; Houston, E.; Boyd, J. T.; Golbe, L.; Bruno, M. K.; Gupta, D. K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: John A. Burns School of Medicine, University of Hawaii
after.abstract: Objective: For the atypical parkinsonian disorders (APDs), including dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and corticobasal degeneration (CBD), accurate antemortem diagnosis remains clinically challenging because of overlapping features, phenotypic heterogeneity, and limited definitive biomarkers. Consensus diagnostic criteria are complex and may not reflect how clinicians operationalize diagnostic reasoning in practice. Methods: We surveyed movement disorders specialists regarding diagnostic implications of 32 clinical features, comparing the results with a 2024 consensus algorithmic framework called the "General Neurologist's Practical Diagnostic Algorithm for APDs". We evaluated inter-rater agreement, diagnosis-level framework coverage, feature-level attribution patterns, and exact-set agreement. Results: Respondents demonstrated strong inter-specialist consensus in feature attribution (raw agreement 81.9%; Gwet's AC1 0.67, 95% CI 0.64-0.70). Specialist endorsement increased markedly with framework association strength, from 12.9% to 36.2% to 82.6% for unmapped, modest, and moderate associations respectively. Diagnosis-level coverage was higher for MSA, PSP, and CBD than for DLB. Exact-set agreement was substantially more variable and depended on whether modest associations were incorporated into the framework definition. Despite high self-reported familiarity with and use of published diagnostic criteria, respondents overwhelmingly expressed interest in a unified diagnostic framework for APDs with automated clinical decision support (CDS). Conclusions: Movement disorders specialists showed internally consistent feature-attribution patterns for archetypal features, while differing in the weighting and breadth assigned to weaker or overlapping associations. These findings are evidence for a gap between consensus schemas and specialist diagnostic reasoning and may inform future diagnostic frameworks and CDS approaches for the APDs.

after.title: Preprint: Assessment of Dissemination in Time in Multiple Sclerosis Using a Single 3D T2-FLAIR magnetic resonance imaging Radiomic Signature
after.authors: GUZMAN, E. G.; Casajuana-Larque, A.; Alberich, M.; Bollo, L.; Mongay-Ochoa, N.; Martinez-Heras, E.; Vidal-Jordana, A.; Montalban, X.; Tintore, M.; Rovira, A.; Sastre-Garriga, J.; Pareto, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Section of Neuroradiology Department of Radiology (IDI) Vall d'Hebron University Hospital
after.abstract: Background: In multiple sclerosis (MS), dissemination in time (DIT) is an important component of demonstrating disease activity and establishing the chronology of lesion development. DIT is routinely assessed from contrast-enhanced or follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Although proved useful, these methods are not without caveats motivating alternative approaches to study lesion chronology. We investigated whether single T2-FLAIR MRI contains sufficient information to distinguish temporally distinct MS lesion categories using radiomic features. Methods: In a retrospective longitudinal cohort of 273 participants with MS (1,311 MRI acquisitions), persistent brain lesions were temporally stratified using serial T2-FLAIR MRI. Long-standing established (LS-E) lesions were defined as observed for six years at least, and recent incident (R-I), as lesions that appeared over the span of two years in a follow-up MRI and were present until the last scan available. Radiomic features were extracted from lesion-level T2-FLAIR MRI. Feature selection was performed in an independent discovery cohort (Group 1, N=55). Selected features were then used to train a support vector machine classifier in a separate development cohort with repeated group-wise cross-validation (Group 2, N=163). Final performance was assessed in an held-out test cohort (Group 3, N=55). An exploratory analysis was then performed on baseline MRI from 64 subjects with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), acquired after their first clinical demyelinating event. Results: Longitudinal tracking identified 814 classifiable lesions in Group 1, 3203 in Group 2, and 984 in Group 3. In Group 1, 18 radiomic features met predefined selection criteria (FDR-adjusted p smaller than 0.05 and absolute Cohen's d greater than 0.8), spanning intensity, shape, and texture domains. In the independent test cohort, the support vector machine classifier achieved an area under the curve of 0.78, with correct classification rates of 66% for R-I lesions and 73% for LS-E lesions. In the exploratory CIS analysis, predicted lesion temporal composition showed substantial inter-patient heterogeneity, with approximately one in ten participants presenting radiomic features compatible with LS-E lesions at their first clinical event. Conclusions: Single T2-FLAIR MRI contains measurable information related to MS lesion chronology. This proof-of-concept framework supports the feasibility of a line of research based on radiomics temporal lesion characterisation without contrast administration or dense longitudinal follow-up MRI, with potential relevance for studying lesion evolution and supporting DIT assessment.

after.title: Preprint: Heterogeneous association between maternal haemoglobin concentration and child haemoglobin levels: a quantile regression analysis using multi-country nationally representative data.
after.authors: Amugsi, D. A.; Osuka, D.; Mwangi, B.; Jomo, S.; Ekiru, S.; Achaliwie, F.; Wilunda, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: African Population and Health Research Center
after.abstract: Background: Low haemoglobin concentration, or anaemia, is a major global public health issue, particularly severe in sub-Saharan Africa, including East Africa, where prevalence rates are alarmingly high. This situation requires a comprehensive analysis to identify the key factors contributing to this high prevalence, especially in East Africa. This study uses robust quantile regression to examine the relationship between maternal haemoglobin concentration and child haemoglobin levels in three East African countries. Methods: The study analysed data from the Demographic and Health Surveys of three East African countries: Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Uganda. These data are nationally representative and are collected every five years from low- and middle-income countries. The analysis included a total sample of 6883 children and their mothers. The primary outcome variable was the haemoglobin concentration of the child. We used quantile regression to model the effects of maternal haemoglobin concentration on child haemoglobin levels, adjusting for potential confounders. Results: A one-unit increase in maternal haemoglobin concentration was associated with a unit increase in child haemoglobin concentration as follows: In Tanzania, the increases were 0.19, 0.20, 0.19, and 0.17 at the 5th, 10th, 25th, and 50th quantiles, respectively. In Ethiopia, the increases were 0.23, 0.22, 0.22, and 0.17 at the same quantiles. In Uganda, the increases were 0.19, 0.19, 0.18, and 0.19 at these quantiles. In contrast, a one-unit increase in maternal Hb concentration was associated with a smaller increase in child haemoglobin concentration, ranging from 0.11 to 0.13 at the 75th and 90th quantiles across all three countries. Overall, the most significant effects of maternal Hb concentration on child Hb levels were observed at the lower end of the conditional Hb distribution in each of the three countries. Conclusion: Maternal haemoglobin concentration is positively associated with children's haemoglobin levels across all countries studied. The strongest association is among children in the lower quantiles, who are at higher risk of anaemia. In contrast, the association is less pronounced among those in the upper quantiles. Therefore, improving maternal haemoglobin is likely to benefit children in the lower quantiles more than those in the upper quantiles. Programmes aimed at addressing child anaemia should consider these differing effects of maternal haemoglobin concentration. Keywords: Haemoglobin concentration, anaemia, maternal, child, quantile regression
